speechtext: The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta on a question of privilege.

subsubtopic: MR. REYNOLDS-REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT AND MEMBER FOR VANCOUVER EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I have given notice, and I have also given notice to the members that it affects. Yesterday during the committee of the whole proceedings on the transportation estimates I was questioning the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) regarding the use of search initiator buoys with respect to which the government passed a regulation to the effect that they should come into operation on July 1 last year. When I asked the minister why they had not come into operation, in his first answer to me he said, as reported at page 677 of Hansard:
There are certain technical problems which we did not overcome. We are trying to solve them and will consider the situation.
I then continued questioning the minister on that and other matters. When I finished my statement I said to the minister that this was an extremely important matter in the province of British Columbia. There are a lot of tugs operating in Canada and people are dying every year because they are being sunk. I wanted to know if he could really give me an answer as to why these regulations had not been put into effect. Although he said previously there had been technical problems, the minister then said to my amazement "the regulations are in effect. There is no
doubt about that." The fact of the matter is that the regulations are not in effect, and I will read a telegram in a moment or two from an individual who is involved and has made a statement on this.
[DOT] (mo)
The question I want to raise now relates to a question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee), and I should like to quote from this statement made yesterday:
A question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. With all due respect to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta, as a member from British Columbia I worked very closely all this time with members of the Canadian Merchant Service Guild on the west coast and made representations to the Department of Transport. They are well aware of the problem that we brought to their attention. As a matter of fact, I just spoke to Captain Arnie Davis who is the Secretary-Treasurer and he indicated to me that the regulations are in force on the west coast.
That statement totally refuted what I had been saying to the minister, that these regulations were not in force and were not being enforced. So, I called Captain Arnie Davis and asked him whether he had made this statement to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee). He was puzzled and sent me a telegram which I should like to read, as I think it refutes what the minister and the hon. member for Vancouver East have said to the effect that the regulations are in force. The telegram reads:
Research initiator buoy regulations. This is to confirm that to the best of my knowledge the named regulations have not and are not in force on the west coast of Canada as of October 22 1974. A.W. Davis Secretary Treasurer western branch Canadian Merchant Service Guild.
That is the same gentleman referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver East in his statement last night. I bring this forward this morning because it is an extremely important matter. While I realize you may say this is argument, these members have made statements in this House that are untrue, and I think we should have some answers from the other side.

subsubtopic: MR. REYNOLDS-REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT AND MEMBER FOR VANCOUVER EAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did speak with Captain Davis this morning about the conversation we had last night. There may be some room for error but I am quite sure I specifically asked him whether the regulations were in force. There may be some indication that we were talking about two separate things, and he may have answered in the affirmative to something else I had asked. When the hon. member asked about that specific aspect I spoke to Mr. Bonn of the Marine Safety Inspection Department this morning and he said the regulations are in effect.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that yesterday in the House the minister said that it would require having a health inspector in every store in the country every day to obtain adequate inspection of meat, and since presumably he could not mean this seriously and was not suggesting that it be taken seriously, I should like to ask the minister in view of what the Chairman of the Food Prices Review Board had to say yesterday on the same subject whether he is reconsidering his position and taking steps to ensure that meat sold at the retail level across the country from time to time will receive adequate inspection.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my statement of yesterday still stands. I might go even further and say that to ensure completely safe meat we would have to almost have an inspector in every house, because there is no guarantee concerning what happens between the time this meat is sold in the store and the time it is consumed. The inspection which is being carried on at the present time is being carried on with all due diligence. As I said yesterday steps have been taken, since the report of the Food Prices Review Board of last June, to improve the situation even further and we will keep on improving it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Minister of Justice. speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGATION MINISTER OF JUSTICE IMPOSING PERSONAL VIEWS ON HOSPITAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to make it clear that the only hospital committee to which I addressed myself in a way that I was aware of was the hospital committee in the Territories for which I am Attorney General, as though I were a provincial attorney general. In the case of other provinces, I drew to the attention of the attorneys general the nature of the 1969 law and the problem that can exist if the hospital committees are not in fact reading that law appropriately. It did seem to me that it was quite appropriate for an attorney general, before launching a prosecution against a hospital committee, to indicate to the hospital committee the problem that exists in regard to applying the law, and this is what I did in the case of the Northern Territories.
It is indeed an important role for an attorney general, in the particular circumstances of the 1969 law, to attempt to see that it is being applied in the way parliament intended. For after all, if we had intended a broader, wide open form of law we would have passed one, but we did not so intend. We put responsibilities upon hospital committees, and I think it is a proper role for attorneys general in this country to make sure that those responsibilities are carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the agreement on procedure, and I am quite happy to go along with anything that the House decides-indeed, I have to do so. I welcome this opportunity, particularly as a new minister and especially as I am new to this portfolio, to discuss the portfolio and its various aspects as well as its estimates with hon. members today. I think that if we can look at it in that light, we can achieve a great deal by finding out what the ministry and its three facets are attempting to do, what the objectives of this House are, and what are the concerns of members of both sides of this House. We have here the blue book. I must say that in the six years I have been a member of parliament I have not really learned how to master that impressive document. However, I am blessed with excellent officials who will be of great assistance.
As hon. members know, there are three principal hats within my portfolio: first, the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs; second, the National Capital Commission, and third, CMHC. I have not recited them in any particular order of importance; they are all equally important, but I have put them in that order because I intend to deal with them in that way.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs is concerned with urban growth and the pattern and quality of that growth in this country. If we look at the projections for this nation, we see that 90 per cent of all Canadians will be living in urban centres by the end of the century. If the present trends are permitted to continue, one third of all Canadians will be living in three major centres around Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal. As great as those cities are, our concern is that such a trend is not desirable, but I think it would be unrealistic to pretend that we can reverse it. However, if we can shape it and manage it in some way, even divert it by as little as 3 per cent, 5 per cent or 7 per cent, that would represent a massive shift. But, more important is that we should decentralize the concentration in these areas to make sure that the quality of the development and of the growth is of a kind that is acceptable and one to which we as Canadians would aspire.
As minister I have great difficulty in determining where "urban" begins and ends because I think it starts on the farm and in the smallest community. Unless these are
702

October 24, 1974
Estimates
vibrant and good places in which to live, people will flock to our cities. Cities are great places in which to live, but I think they should be places of choice and people should not be pressured into moving into those centres. There are different ways of approaching this matter. We are concerned about the quality of life both in the smaller communities and in the larger centres, but especially in the cores of those communities.
The Ministry of State for Urban Affairs set up some three years ago is relatively new. My two distinguished predecessors have been experienced, able and sensitive ministers and they have established the trilevel process which means that all levels of government confer together about problems of mutual interest in relation to the urban fact in this country. This is not an easy process. The provinces and municipalities have their jurisdictions which they guard jealously. It is not by accident that they are there. I think there is something valuable in our system of government which allows each of us to deal on a priority basis with those matters which we can best handle. I reject the term "senior and junior levels of government" because I do not think they are really applicable. They are just different levels of government, and a case could be made for each level being the most important. They are all important and different, and the trilevel process helps to bring us together in a mutual cause to discuss matters of mutual interest and learn where each fits and can help the other.
Perhaps one of the most significant moves as a result of the second trilevel conference in Edmonton was the establishment of an independent trilevel task force on municipal finances headed by Dr. Deutsch. This is very important because municipalities themselves have been deeply concerned about their tax base. I do not think anyone acknowledges that a proper tax base is the most equitable, the best that can be devised, but we do not know what the answers are. Some people suggest federal tax transfers or provincial tax transfers, but I think we all recognize the fact that it is very easy to spend money that someone else provides. It is the very essence of our democratic system that we are elected to carry out the trust of the people. In some ways I think we should be called trustees rather than members of parliament. We initiate programs and tax people for the money to implement those programs. We take responsibility for that at election time or, conversely, we do not implement programs and we do not tax people, and we take the responsibility for that also.
I feel deeply, therefore, that it is important that the level of government which spends should also take the responsibility for that taxation. I could go on to give examples of other jurisdictions with other municipal income taxes. Strangely enough, they have not been all that successful, as I have found in speaking to the mayor of one of our major cities this morning. The municipalities have the responsibility for taxing, but it becomes a very different thing when you leave that responsibility to someone else and you just have the responsibility for spending. That is fundamental to our system of responsible government.
Then, why don't you bring the estimates back to the House?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
There are other things in the ministry which are of particular interest. One is the railroad relocation and crossing act which offers a unique opportunity to the provinces and municipalities to join us in redeveloping, particularly central cores, regenerating them where they have been blighted by railways, and making them into better communities in which to live. Certainly, we must co-ordinate the federal presence which is considerable in most urban centres. Federal land holdings are considerable. There are some 200,000 acres of federally owned land in urban centres across Canada which are not usable for housing but which could be strategic land if used for recreation in the development of cities and towns. We have established a special policy of land management in the federal government and hon. members might be interested in this.
First, the federal government will, by and large, no longer sell its land holdings which are surplus to needs of government departments. Public lands will remain as much as possible in the public domain so the public has a basic decision to make on that land use.
Second, when a government property is no longer required by the department which is using it, a rapid examination will be made by the urban affairs ministry to determine what should be the best use of that land in urban terms. This will ensure that the redevelopment of federal properties takes place in the light of urban rather than purely narrow financial considerations.
Third, all important federal land holdings in major cities will be systematically reviewed on a cyclical basis to ensure they are being put to best urban use. I could go on at great length, Mr. Chairman, on the urban affairs aspect of my portfolio which is included in the estimates today and this may come out in my discussions.
I should like to mention the National Capital Commission because it is of special interest to members of parliament and to all Canadians. In my list of priorities, the capital city must first of all be a good place in which to live and work; that is the primary function of an urban centre. Second, it must be the capital city for all Canadians. All Canadians must feel at home here, must feel comfortable here, no matter what region they come from or what their mother tongue. We have development plans for the core area and the linking of the Ottawa and Hull regions. We have a regional plan as well for the greater national capital region.
I hope all hon. members have read the annual report issued last week by the National Capital Commission. It suggests some very interesting things and puts forward some good ideas for the national capital region. We will shortly be issuing the concept plan of the National Capital Commission. This looks at the development of the area for the next three decades. It follows the Greber plan which has been used over the last 20 years. We now have an opportunity for a new approach. We also have the Fullerton approach which deals with the governmental structure for the region. These present a unique opportunity to examine the reports and the expertise that have accumulated, and it is for that reason that in the Speech from the Throne we proposed a joint committee of federal

October 24, 1974

houses to study the national capital plan, the concept plan, the Fullerton report and any other information that comes to hand. I think we all have a special interest in this.
I strongly suspect that hon. members are primarily concerned with the housing situation today, although I hope it is not their only concern. I think the record of this government gives us reason for pride as Canadians, though not for complacency, of course. The Economic Council of Canada said that over a five-year period, from 1968 to 1973, it would be necessary to build millions of homes in Canada. That was quite a challenge. As a matter of fact, as a candidate in 1968 I said that if we did not achieve that objective I would not stand again as a candidate for my party.
Then, you had better sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: No, we have exceeded that goal year by year. We have exceeded 200,000 homes every single year and have established records one after the other.
Hear, hear!
Relate that to population change.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
This is quite a good rate of progress. In the six years there have been 1,350,000 homes and in the same period there have been 700,000 new family formations. Quality of housing has also improved, although there are naturally areas of concern. We still have a long way to go with those who are socially deprived, who have financial and economic problems, and with the native peoples and others.
Quantity itself is not enough. There must be quality of housing and good distribution in all regions and at all economic levels. Our concern must be for those who are most vulnerable and not able to afford housing. Some people suggest housing has been used as an economic tool, but if you look at the budget you will find that each year more money has gone into housing.
The new program which came into being in 1973 was in operation for only half of that year and our capital commitments for that year were $923 million. The capital budget for 1974, the first full year of the revised act, is $1,262 million. Of this budget, 77 per cent is committed to housing programs and the balance for land, sewage facilities and other operations considered as infrastructure. Of the housing budget, 95 per cent has gone into low cost housing for people who cannot normally afford it and some of the 5 per cent balance has gone in CMHC's role as lender of last resort in regions where lending institutions are not normally active. A high proportion of the 5 per cent has also gone into low and moderate priced housing.
One of the most interesting innovations of my predecessor was the Assisted Home Ownership Plan, or AHOP. Some people said it would not work because the price limits were not realistic, that they were too low. But a funny thing happened on the way to the forum, Mr. Chairman. People started to look for housing in the price range and, because of tight money, builders realized this was where they could get funds so they started to build houses within the price range. It has had the effect of supplying homes and bringing down the price. We know that in many major centres prices were set at what the traffic
Estimates
would bear and not necessarily related to the cost. In 1974, $300 million was budgeted for that program and its success resulted in a substantial increase of the budget. It produced some 20,000 homes for 80,000 or 90,000 Canadians. Part of that was for existing housing and part of it for new housing.
It soon became apparent that the success of this program was one of its greatest problems, and that we would have to increase the supply of funds. In effect, we had to make a trade-off. Rather than have the program work simply for people getting housing, we wanted to use what funds were left to increase the housing stock. I know it is a disappointment to some people that it was not continued for existing housing but I felt that we had to conserve our resources and use them where they would be most effective. During my term as minister, this is the approach I will be taking-to get the maximum leverage out of the taxpayer's dollar.
Public housing in this country has been a great success. In the last six years the stock has been increased substantially and more housing has been produced in this period than in the previous 22 years. That is not a bad record.
It is still only one per cent of the total housing stock.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend mentions the one per cent figure. I understand his concern, as I know the constituency he represents. We need new housing. We are not producing old new houses, if I may use that term. We need new houses. As far as we are concerned, 95 per cent will go to those income groups we have mentioned.
I am concerned about the reluctance of municipalities to accept public housing. I think politicians can give leadership in this field. People must not be gun-shy and say "No, we do not want these people in public housing in our area". Some people respond too quickly this way, and the solution requires leadership.
You cannot lead people who do not want to be led. Through leadership we must provide a voice which will be responded to in the community, so that we may develop a cohesive housing policy for the betterment of society. This will not come about by itself. It needs people to do it. We must recognize that this is a problem we must all face. We must also realize that there is a need for public housing. The attitude of people should not be, "Let them build public housing in an area other than mine." We cannot approach our problems in that fashion. On the other hand, if we accept our responsibilities we will become mutually enriched.
I could talk about non-profit and cooperative housing, which is a relatively new national force in the housing picture and deserves attention. The program is not increasing housing stock very much, but it is an important factor.
Let me say this, Mr. Chairman. In the field of housing the government of Canada is not standing still. We have an immense number of programs at work. There is no simple solution to our problems. We can talk about lending guarantees, public housing, senior citizens' houses, student housing, land assembly programs and services,
28305-45'/;

October 24, 1974
Estimates
AHOP, our limited dividend rental programs, our cooperative housing, our mortgage investment corporation, the registered home ownership savings plan, of which I will speak more later, programs like NIP, RRAP, programs for rural housing, and so on. As I say there is an immense number of programs which can help us do the job and which we have modified and improved as we go along. I welcome hon. members' questions, so that we can discuss these things together.

Mr. Chairman, may I congratulate the minister on his new position. I have known him since he came to the House. I think all will agree with me when I say he is an affable person. He will do the best he can in the circumstances, as all will agree, I think.
The minister faces vast problems. The previous minister, to whom I was not quite so kind, was full of puffery but little came of it. That is what prompted us at the beginning of the session to ask questions about housing.
In the 20 minutes allotted to me I will talk about the housing crisis and see if we cannot arrive at some solutions. I will ask the minister some questions and expect short answers. So many questions need to be answered and only the minister and his departmental officials can help us.
First, the minister must accept that there is a crisis in housing. Why is there a crisis in housing? In responding to a question asked on October 2, the minister implied that there is no housing crisis, even though housing starts this year are down by 24.3 per cent. Although the minister said in the House that there is no housing crisis, he said the contrary when interviewed by Southam News Services on October 21. According to the article by Guy Demarino:
Danson says he's 'about to present new ideas to cabinet' to help solve the housing mess. But any new ideas will take considerable time to be explained, developed, discussed, accepted, and financed-
Danson also wants his cabinet colleagues to support a plan, under which public subsidies would be linked to private capital and lead to more homebuilding. The government would, under the plan, subsidize private lenders to bring the effective mortgage rate down to AHOP levels.
Clearly, the minister thinks there is a housing mess. It is no use talking about AHOP. Of the $500 million allocated, $437 million has been spent. The minister must go to the Minister of Finance and others who control the economy for more money. But they say "no, we are cutting back; we are in a tight money situation." So, I understand his moaning. The problem is truly great.
How many wage earners are buying new houses? According to the Toronto Star, about five per cent of wage earners at one time bought new houses. That figure has now sunk to zero. Wage earners cannot afford high-priced housing and the highest mortgage interest rate in history. In Vancouver, for example, because the vacancy rate has dropped almost to nil, rents are going up. Wage earners are going to the boss and saying, "Give us more money; we need it to pay higher rents."
Houses are not selling. Why? According to law firms across the country, CMHC and conventional mortgage loans are running at better than 11 per cent. If you lack the full down payment and need a second mortgage, you will pay between 18 per cent and 20 per cent. I foresee a decline in our economy and there will be more foreclo-

sures in housing than this country has ever seen. Without exaggerating, what happened in the '30s will look like prosperity. The minister does not control money. The real demons are his colleagues who will do nothing about inflation. So, when he spoke today, it was like sneezing in a dust storm. It meant nothing.
Now, let me ask some questions. Housing starts in 1974, compared with 1973, are down by 24.3 per cent, according to Statistics Canada. Why are these housing starts down? The chairman of the Conference Board of Canada looked forward to one million extra houses being built by this year. Yet housing starts have fallen below 200,000. That figure was picked out five or six years ago by the Economic Council of Canada. I want to ask the minister why housing starts are down and what action is being taken to meet this situation outside AHOP. Incidentally, I hope the hon. gentleman does not mention that word while he is replying to my questions, because it means nothing-he cannot get any money out of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member obviously recognizes that the basic problem is inflation, and he does not accept that the record of the present government compares more than favourably with that of any other government in the world in this regard. As I say, the real problem is inflation, which brings us to high interest rates. Despite this, our completions this year will be in the range of 250,000. Understandably, the hon. member is concerned about next year.
The admonition not to mention AHOP is unfortunately, I think, because the program has been highly successful. It would be unfair to exclude it when it is providing something like 20,000 units. Incidentally, the decline is not in new dwellings; the real concern is for rental accommodation in the coming year-multiple unit structures. This is where the emphasis will be placed, and I would draw attention to Section 15 of the National Housing Act which brings in the private sector. Possibly new methods will be required so that the immense resources in private funds available for housing can be directed to that field at lower rates. If we are to bring these rates down, it will be by subsidy. That is my objective-to bring the private lending institutions into the field. They have the funds, but cannot get them out working today because of the high interest rates.

I notice that according to the newspaper article the minister talked about subsidizing interest rates. I also noted, in the same article, that the Minister of Finance had said that in no way are there to be any subsidies. So, we are locked in.
I should like to ask the minister two questions. The first relates to the $100 million a year for land acquisition about which the former minister used to spread his chest. How much of that sum has been allocated and where were the land banks established-if anything was done at all? Has a further $100 million been allocated for this year? As we all know, the cost of land is the demon when we get into the realm of housing. In brief, how much was spent, where was it spent and does the minister have another $100 million this year?
October 24, 1974

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: This is a new program and I appreciate the hon. member's recognition of its importance. It is being applied right across Canada. It is not the intention to fund strictly $100 million a year; the program calls for $500 million over five years. I believe we have exceeded the $100 million in the last couple of years. In reply to the hon. member's question, perhaps I should begin by giving the figure for Alberta, which is $690,000. Then, Newfoundland . .. This can't be right surely-$6,910,000. Yes, that makes up the total. Newfoundland, $6,910,000. I didn't believe what I saw. But it shows what a Liberal government can do when there is a strong opposition.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Ontario, $19 million; British Columbia, $3 million. And so on. So this money is going out. The program is going on stream and we are just beginning to see the results. There is a terrific time lag here, as I am sure the hon. member would appreciate. But the program is going on stream.

The list the minister gave is still far short of $100 million. Alberta, $6 million, British Columbia $6 million, Ontario, $19 million-that is a long way from a $100 million. But is $100 million set aside this year?
I want to turn now, to the demonstration program. This involved $100 million to be spread over five years to finance what we call innovative programs. The intention was to look at new technological methods of cutting housing costs. As I pointed out in the House this scheme would cost more than $54,000 a day for every day it was in operation. I should like to know what experimental project has been carried out with that $100 million and where it has been built, outside one situated in the former minister's constituency, perhaps, to impress the voters.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: First, as to the land assembly program. If the provinces respond there will certainly be another $100 million available this year for that purpose. As to the urban demonstration program, nothing as yet has been spent out of this fund. It is a very serious program. As the hon. member implied when one is spending $54,000 plus change a day it has to be treated seriously. This program extends over a five year period. An advisory committee consisting of highly qualified professionals has been set up, not to build any sort of gimmickry, or to build in any particular constituencies, but to put in concrete form real responses to urban problems. The committee knows I intend to be rather tough in this connection because I have the ultimate responsibility. This is to result not in any great schemes which will benefit mankind but in specific projects in Canadian urban centres or around them, for the benefit of Canadians. Purely theoretical exercises will not be considered. I know this is the feeling of the advisory committee as well. The first funding will be next year.

So nothing has yet been spent out of this $100 million. It has not built one house. It seems to me that this money should have been spent to help people build houses.
Let me draw the minister's attention to some figures I have here-these are put out by Statistics Canada. The cost of new houses in Canada has risen by 60.7 per cent in
Estimates
the last five years compared with 38 per cent in the United States. Mortgage interest rates in Canada have gone up by 76.9 per cent compared with 18.4 per cent in the United States. The cost of property insurance rose by 130 per cent in Canada though it rose by only 13 per cent in the United States. I could go on and on to show how inflation in Canada has eaten away the resources of the little man until he can no longer afford proper shelter.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit an observation in relation to those statistics?

I want to put one more question. The minister can comment then, if he wishes, at the same time as he replies to what I have to say. I am far from happy about the Prime Minister telling us he intended to give people $500 in lieu of not abolishing the 11 per cent sales tax. Then, during the election campaign, he said that the government would do it in the next four years. I ask the minister, how many Canadians have yet received these $500 cheques? I suggest not one. It is like an innovative program. Let me ask the minister whether he has any legislation ready yet to carry out this promise, or is this another election bluff like the promise to curb inflation?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it is worth observing, though I have not checked the statistics in this regard, that United States housing starts have dropped 50 per cent, compared with 23 per cent or 24 per cent in this country. I think that is of particular significance. Our policies have produced housing, theirs have not. I am not suggesting that we do not have problems, but I do not think that the situation is a crisis. Rather it is a problem, but a problem with which we can cope. Obviously, with housing starts dropping off south of the border almost 50 per cent, in what is one of the most advanced nations of the world, this is an indication that we are doing better. With regard to the $500 in lieu of sales tax, this is something that we have under active consideration. It was a commitment.
It was a promise.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and I hope to be making an announcement within the next several days in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few minutes left so may I just say this. I could go on all day asking the minister questions, but they all add up to one thing. The government has been full of words not deeds. In light of the fact that Canadians are now unable to get proper shelter, and in light of the fact that real estate agents are not selling houses, would the minister look into an outfit called Rentex. People looking for a home pay this outfit $50 to find a home for them and they have a monopoly all across the nation. I would ask that action be taken under the Combines Investigation Act.
I should also like to see an investigation in connection with a certain development around Calgary concerning the amalgamation of four or five companies. Not only is this happening in Calgary but it is happening in other cities, too. I did receive a letter from the president of a company in my area who complained about what was

October 24, 1974
Estimates
going on. Therefore, I ask the minister to look into this situation for the good of Canada and Canadians. I will now sit down since my time is up, and may I say I appreciate the courtesy of the minister for taking the time with me, even though he was unable to give me all the answers.

Mr. Chairman, last July and August I would have had no difficulty complimenting the Minister of State for Urban Affairs on his appointment. He is a very affable, likeable and competent type of person. But he has been a cabinet minister now for almost four months, and on the basis of his performance in that short period, and also the attitude of the government to one of the most serious problems facing the country today, the serious housing shortage, I am convinced he is really trying to smile and bluff, certainly from having listened to him for 20 minutes this morning. The housing crisis has rather serious consequences for most Canadians. I think that instead of becoming minister of housing he is becoming minister of hoaxing. He is pulling a cruel hoax so far as his attitude to, and inaction in, the housing field is concerned.
Why do I say that, Mr. Chairman? First of all, let me look at the Liberal promises made during the election. First was the $500 tax free grant to first time purchasers of new homes. The answer of the minister in the last five minutes was that this matter was still under active consideration. An amount of $500 is very small in light of the dramatic increase that has taken place in the cost of housing during the last few years. In fact, in the year 1973 the increase in the cost of lumber and wood products amounted to $800 for the average home. The minister now says he has under active consideration a $500 grant to first time purchasers of new homes.
May I mention to the minister that if he were to remove the 11 per cent sales tax, not on all homes but particularly on homes priced in the moderate to middle income bracket, there would be a saving of $1,300 on the average home. From the minister's answer to the hon. member for Huron yesterday in regard to this grant, I have come to the conclusion that the minister is trying to bluff and smile his way through this serious problem.
Secondly, I remind the minister of another election promise of the Liberal party, namely that they would direct more national housing mortgage moneys into moderately priced homes with low down payments. This was given great thrust when the Prime Minister made his western trip. May I tell the minister that the limits set were so low that they would exclude virtually every house now on sale in our cities. That was the second promise of the Liberal party.
Thirdly, they said there would be a provision to allow homeowners to pay off mortgages in the first five years without excessive pre-payment penalty. The Prime Minister and speakers for the Liberal party made sure not to define the word "excessive". The question now arises, why should the average homeowner have to pay a penalty because he wants to pay off his mortgage within the first five years? This indicates the cruel attitude of the minister to people who are struggling to pay off their mortgages.
May I continue at two o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

AFTER RECESS

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. When the committee rose at one o'clock the estimates of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs were under consideration, as found at pages 29 and 30 of schedule A of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, at the time of the adjournment I had stated that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs had changed his concept from that of minister of housing to that of minister of hoaxing. I suggest the reason for that is inaction by the government respecting the serious housing problem across the country. I gave as examples of inaction of the government the lack of action on the $500 grant for first-time purchasers of homes, and the government's attitude regarding NHA participating more in the mortgage field across the country, especially in respect of low-income families. The government set the limit so low that virtually no one in a city could take advantage of the program set forth by the Prime Minister during the election campaign. I also said that the government's idea of allowing home owners to pay for mortgages in the first five years without excessive prepayment penalty had not been put into effect by the government.
The fourth Liberal promise during the election campaign was a change in the NHA regulations permitting CMHC to buy land and lease it to co-operative and nonprofit housing organizations. The record in respect of this promise has been dismal failure. The president of CMHC said there is reluctance to provide funds, on the basis that projects could be unprofitable. The question of profit is hardly a criterion for co-operative housing. We have witnessed Toronto city officials and officials of the Ontario Federation of Labour coming to Ottawa to persuade the minister to become more active in supplying funds for non-profit housing and co-operatives. That action has been very slow.
The fifth Liberal promise during the election campaign was in respect of regional and local ceilings on NHA mortgages. This was to be done by regulation, but there has been no action to adjust the rates of NHA mortgages pertaining to different regions across the country. Those were the election promises.
Let me now come to the performance of the Liberal government and the lack of action by the minister of hoaxing. Regarding the supply of housing, there has been a dramatic decrease in the number of house completions and it is now almost certain, qs the hon. member for Calgary North said, that in 1974 there will be a drop of approximately 20 to 25 per cent in house completions. This means a loss of $1.5 billion in wages and salaries to Canadian workers. Goodness knows, we have a serious unemployment situation especially in the forest products industry of British Columbia and Quebec where these men could be employed.
October 24, 1974

I am sure the minister knows that developers in large cities said in the spring of 1974 they would not build multiple units because their return did not compare with the return on land speculation or on the construction of single-family dwellings. We experienced a dramatic drop in housing starts because developers found they could make more profit on land speculation and building singlefamily houses. We have a serious crisis in housing rental units, especially in the large cities.
Today the minister pounded his chest as he talked about the Assisted Home Ownership Program.
Not too hard, I hope.

The minister failed to mention that the substance of the proposal made during the election campaign was to raise the subsidy from $25 to $50 and that the eligibility limit for the subsidy was to be even lower for NHA mortgages. The limit in British Columbia was $32,000 before one became eligible for AHOP, and $30,000 in Ottawa, yet experience has shown that you can hardly buy the necessary land in our larger cities for that amount of money.
With respect to the cost of housing the record of this government is even more miserable and dismal. The cost of land and the cost of mortgage money have risen at a tremendous rate. Last year we heard what the Liberals and the Tories said when the Residential Mortgages Financing Act was passed. It was supposed to stabilize the flow of money by making mortgages more attractive. That was the purpose of the bill. Since the passage of that bill last year we have seen the conventional mortgage interest rate increase from 9.5 per cent to 13 per cent. This is what the Tories and Liberals did when they brought in the act to make mortgages more attractive.
In respect of the price of homes we have seen a slight drop because of buyer resistance to the cost of homes and the high interest rate. There has been a drop in Toronto from $57,000 to $55,000 for the average house. When I travelled through my constituency during the election campaign I was amazed at the number of empty houses owned by speculators which had "For sale" signs on them. The reason was that most of these houses were in the $45,000 range and required a mortgage of at least $35,000. To obtain a $35,000 mortgage on a 25-year basis, at a rate of interest of 11 per cent, would require monthly payments of principal and interest of $336.89. In other words, if you take yearly payments of $4042.68 for a period of 25 years, it totals $100,670.
Is it not obvious why there is such resistance to buying homes in our large cities? I now refer to the minister's attitude toward housing. We in the New Democratic Party say that every person is entitled to decent housing at reasonable cost. This has also been stated by the Social Development Council and, as the hon. member for Don Valley reminds me, by the federal task force. Let us consider the attitude of the minister. He suggests that people must choose whether to buy a house or have extras such as a car, boat, or other luxuries. He says that they cannot have both. I would remind the minister that many Canadians cannot have either; they cannot have a house or
Estimates
the luxuries he speaks about. I am amazed at his philosophy.
What is the minister's solution? He said he would encourage developers, through tax incentives, to build houses. He has the limited dividend section of the act through which he hopes to encourage them to build. I would remind the minister that in the last six years limited dividend housing has never passed 5 per cent of the total housing for the year. There was one exception, in 1970, when the sum of $200 million was directed toward smaller lots with smaller homes for Canadians.
This is the second part of the minister's philosophy. He has taken no action with regard to interest rate increases. He has done nothing in respect of a land bank. He has done nothing with regard to the $500 bonus plan. He has done nothing regarding the 11 per cent sales tax on certain housing. He has taken no action in respect of the 50 per cent capital gains tax, which should be at least 100 per cent. He has done nothing with regard to Indian and Metis housing in Canada. This is a very disgraceful performance.
My time is limited, but I must tell the minister what we in the New Democratic Party would do if we were facing the problems he faces. I shall sum it up in five sentences. First, we would bring land under public ownership and development through a $3 billion revolving fund for the acquisition of development land around our major cities. Second, we would institute a 100 per cent capital gains tax on land sales, with an additional surtax on speculative holdings of less than five years, in order to bring down the cost of acquisitions. Third, we would provide 100 per cent funding to provinces and municipalities to service land holdings. Fourth, we would provide 6 per cent mortgages for low and moderate income families. Fifth, there would be direct government intervention to ensure an adequate supply of moderately priced housing either through contracting out to private builders or, where necessary, construction by a government agency.
Mr. Chairman, I should like the minister to take the initiative and change his philosophy so there would be a major thrust toward having Canadians decently housed at reasonable cost. I would rather call him a minister of housing than a minister of hoaxing. At the moment I would say he is perpetrating a cruel hoax on many Canadians.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when one considers the responsibilities of the Minister of State in the field of housing and urban affairs, and the cheerful responses the minister offers the House, one is tempted to ask the popular question: Why is that man smiling? I have nothing but good wishes for the new minister. I would not want him to misunderstand me. I respect his talent and his good humour. I am very much afraid, however, that he is already falling very quickly into the complacent attitude that many of his senior colleagues in the administration have made a hallmark of this administration. If he could be redeemed from that fate before the cement sets hard around him, I would be very happy. This is one of the main reasons for my intervention today. It would be a shame to see a new minister, particularly one in this portfolio, become lost in the attitude that everything must be right after all because the Liberals are still in power.

October 24, 1974
Estimates
There is much to be disturbed about in this country's affairs. A good portion of what disturbs me revolves around the government's cynicism, and repeated examples of it, in the realm of housing. Over the last couple of years the government frequently has said one thing and done another. It has promised, then deferred, and then done nothing more. Now we have a new minister along with the most recent flock of unfulfilled promises.
It seems to me that the minister and the government expect us and the Canadian people to sit around and wait for something to happen at some time in the future. I do not think that is good enough. The Prime Minister might well like us to believe that he is keeping his word when he states that the housing program promised during the election campaign will be implemented in the course of the life of this parliament-some four or five years-but his government will not in fact be meeting its responsibilities if it does not show determined leadership in bringing forward a housing policy at least to attack the immediate problems.
It seems to me the kind of policy required must be comprehensive and must involve more than simply some inventions by CMHC. It will require the co-ordinated effort of every department of government including, of course, housing, urban affairs, manpower, immigration, Indian Affairs and certainly finance. The minister may say we are not in a housing crisis-as he is fond of saying-but certainly we face a crisis in housing right now, a compounded crisis both in terms of cost and supply, because housing starts are down significantly and costs are up very dramatically. In five years-I think my figures are right-the cost of new housing has increased by over 60 per cent, according to Statistics Canada. That is just in respect of houses. If you include land costs, the increase over a period of five years for a new property including land is almost 110 per cent on average. Over the same period, mortgage interest rates have increased by almost 77 per cent.
A year ago we could see that housing prices and mortgage interest rates were increasing beyond the reach of most Canadians. One did not have to be very smart to see that. We could see, also that the housing market was becoming more and more an inflation shelter for those who could afford that kind of investment as hedge against inflationary expectations. The NDP member who just finished speaking said that in many instances it became a source of speculation and a hedge against inflation. Over and over again we and others warned the government that this was happening and that the little guy was being crushed in the process. There was no appropriate response from the government. Indeed, it was months before the government even conceded that our analysis was accurate.
Then, of course, we had the election campaign, bringing forth a flurry of activity, a basket of promises and AHOP. AHOP was made more generous. It had to be, because it certainly had become a rather sick joke the way it was operating. But now AHOP is all the minister talks about. Ask the minister the time of day and he will tell you about AHOP. The government's tactics, so far as defence is concerned, are "A HOP" a skip and a jump.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister appeared on the television program "Question Period" and said that in order to deliver houses and apartments at an economic price we must accept some compromises; that there are certain trade-offs which we might have to accept-for instance, green spaces. On October 7, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton asked the minister to clarify what this meant. The minister replied, in one of his more illuminating statements, as follows:
This is an ongoing discussion with provincial and municipal officials as well as other people in Canada. Certainly, we have to treat this with great sensitivity, and I put as high a priority on parks and recreation as on any other element in the housing field.
He made it sound better.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He may have made it sound better, but there was no more substance to it. I do not believe that the minister's answer clarified his earlier statement, and I say very frankly to him through you, Mr. Chairman, that I do not like what seems to be the general direction of the minister's thinking in this regard. I do not accept the position that provision of adequate serviced land will require the diminution or the reduction of green spaces in our cities. I say this as emphatically as I can, because it is very hard to get green spaces in cities. I do not know of any city in Canada which has too many of them, and I do not want to see green spaces lost through some alleged short gain.
To put it another way, I do not believe that the preservation of green spaces in existence precludes the adequate provision of land for home or apartment construction. The green spaces we now enjoy in our urban areas in no way caused the severe housing problems that we are now facing, and they must not be compromised as part of some half-baked solution to our problem of making available enough serviced land. I say, sir, that in this country there is no excuse for that kind of trade-off. The open spaces we have to do something about are not the green, open spaces in our cities but, rather, the gaping holes in the policies of the minister and the government. Who knows what the housing policy of this government really is? Is there any contingency planning to meet the crisis? There does not seem to be, from any evidence that I have seen. We are geared to conditions which generally do not apply now, if they ever did. Take the explosion in the price of land for residential development. It stands directly in the way of tens of thousands of ordinary, hard working families who want to own their own homes. I believe these people are justified in not viewing such prices as a necessary or acceptable burden.
The president of CMHC stated recently that the government is using all the devices that are available to increase the supply of serviced land. He said that the government could intervene heavily if housing starts fall much below
200,000	next year, but not before. Mr. Teron expressed the view that this number of starts is enough to allow us to hold our own without making any substantial improvement in the general living conditions of Canadians.
Does this government now believe that times are so good with respect to housing that it should do nothing more than make certain that things do not get any worse? Is
October 24, 1974

that the attitude of the minister and of the government? I say that this country has every right to expect something better. For far too many low and middle income Canadians, the situation is quite intolerable. The government has, indeed, a moral obligation to avert shortages and another escalation, in prices next year and to improve vastly the situation which we are already experiencing.
With regard to land prices in particular, I believe that a major thrust is necessary to improve this situation and to ensure an orderly and adequate expansion of our housing stocks. The government, in conjunction with the provinces, must provide the resources to do that job, and provide them now. I say to the minister that this would be an investment in social and urban progress and, furthermore, it would both moderate inflationary pressures in this field and generate employment. The minister responsible for housing and urban affairs and the Minister of Finance should be launching such an initiative without delay. We will be looking for comprehensive responses and answers.
It will come in the budget.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will not wait for the budget. I am tired of sitting around waiting for the budget and I dare say the Canadian people are also darned tired of waiting for the budget. The Conference Board in Canada has predicted that if the government continues with its present approach-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The windbag over there can just settle down. I don't know whether he was moved down to that corner so as not to disturb the House too much.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We are getting a draught here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Conference Board has predicted that if the government continues its present policy, we will witness a further decline in housing starts next year. If nothing is done quickly, and if the present trend continues, a severe housing shortage will develop by mid-1975, according to the board, and as we move into 1975 completions will begin to fall off unless the decline in new housing starts is reversed. Without such reversal the supply of new housing will be very tight after mid-1975, and that will inevitably lead to further upward pressures on rents and on housing prices. I suppose that is the government's anti-inflationary program. If we now had more adequate inventories of shelter in major areas, this restriction in supply would not be too drastic in its effects. But on the contrary, inventories in most urban areas are at extremely low levels.
A recent report of the Economic Council of Canada, entitled "Toward more stable growth in construction", contains the following words:
Our analysis indicates that more stable growth in housing starts would significantly retard future increases in housing costs.
That is something which any government with the slightest interest in fighting inflation and helping the
Estimates
people should bear in mind. I continue reading from the report:
With increased stability in residential construction, therefore, more and better housing could be financially accessible to the poor, and all participants in housing construction itself would probably also benefit.
I would hope that this government would at least do something to help housing and fight inflation apart from talking about the problem being international. Here is a lead for the minister. The report went on to say its findings indicate that a good part of the instability in housing construction stems from over-all instability in the economy and the instability of government monetary policies in particular. The Minister of Finance himself recognized this relationship when he said in the memorable May 6 budget address:
Rates of interest are high, but the way to bring them down is to slow the rate of inflation. This will take time. Meanwhile, I expect the banks to continue to give preference in their lending to small business, mortgage finance for housing and borrowers in the less-favoured regions of the country.
However, sir, expectations are not policy and the Minister of Finance's management of the Canadian economy has led us, among other things, into another classic boom and bust cycle in housing construction. The severity of the problem and its impact on our society calls for effective action and we are not getting it. One reason the mortgage market is so difficult for someone trying to build a new home is apparent. In August, 1971, the percentage of NHA guaranteed mortgages being used to finance the purchase of existing homes was 5.6 per cent; in August, 1972, it was 8.5 per cent. In August, 1974, the percentage of NHA approved guaranteed mortgages being utilized for the purchase of existing homes, rather than building new homes, was 45.4 per cent. That was 45.4 per cent, Mr. Chairman, of NHA guaranteed mortgages being used, not to help purchase new homes but to help purchase existing homes. That is easy to understand, because the old mortgages which might have been on the existing homes were completely inadequate in view of inflated prices when the homes came on the market. This indicates the scope of the problem which the minister faces, and he just seems to be trying to smile it away.
Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister talks about leadership, and the Minister of Finance tells us time and time again that supply is the cornerstone of the government's anti-inflation program. Where is the supply policy for housing? It does not exist. Where is the comprehensive, anti-inflationary policy which is necessary to stabilize prices and mortgage interest rates? Where is the great leadership we heard so much about?
In France.

I hope he will face up to these problems, because there is no time to waste.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the minister upon his appointment and hope he discharges his tremendous responsibilities with the courage needed to meet them. Before I speak about housing, I want to comment on what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said yesterday in suggesting that the condemnation of government spending should not be too great. He lectured us and said civilizations progress by spending money.
Let me say this. The times when civilizations have not made progress have been those when people have lacked confidence in the ability of their elected members to spend their money wisely and effectively. Unless we deal with estimates responsibly and effectively, we shall run into serious problems. Anyone who thinks that the estimates are handled properly in House of Commons committees obviously has never attended a committee meeting. Until the opposition is given proper staff, and until estimates are considered in the House of Commons, we shall see uncontrolled and improper spending, not because of fraud but because the estimates are not examined as people have every right to expect they will be.
I am delighted to have this opportunity to speak on schedule B concerning Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, found on page 30 of the bill. I am speaking on vote 10 which has to do with our total housing program and policy. I was astonished to hear the minister say this morning that there is no serious problem in housing. I should not have been surprised, however, because that is how members of the government talk about any difficult situation. We are getting to the stage with this government where there are no standards, no goals with respect to inflation and housing.
I cannot understand a minister who comes from the Toronto area suggesting that there is no housing problem in the urban areas of our country. I cannot understand other senior ministers suggesting that. Today the apartment vacancy rate in metropolitan Toronto is probably below 1 per cent, and everyone knows that unless a vacancy rate is 5 per cent, the rental market will not function properly. Allowing a vacancy rate that low to develop means that the housing problems of those in the rental market will be particularly severe this winter. Rents are rising. The standard rule of thumb used to be that one should not spend more than 20 per cent of one's income on rent. Today in Toronto people are paying 30 per cent, 40 per cent and, in the case of low income groups, up to 50 per cent of income for rent. That is a shameful situation. It
October 24, 1974

brings degradation and real hardship to people with low incomes.
It has always been argued that people should not spend more than 214 times their income on housing. The average family income in Toronto is about $12,000, which means that the average house should sell for $30,000. There are no houses for $30,000 in the area. People can no longer afford a home. Housing for middle income groups is not being built. It does not exist in our metropolitan areas.
At one time in this country people could choose their type of accommodation. Some like to rent, some to own. They cannot choose today. The difficulty is that they cannot find accommodation at all which is commensurate with their income. Considering our low density of population and the fact that we have all the things we need to build houses, the present situation is puzzling. How can one explain this very serious situation? I suppose the minister will blame it on inflation. Why should inflation cause our housing problems? Has inflation created the present housing situation? Even though the Minister of Finance thinks that inflation exists somewhere in the upper atmosphere, it is clear that not all inflation is imported.
If we want housing, we have all the land and materials we need. So why should we see in Toronto the highest housing prices on the north American continent? It makes no sense. You cannot blame our difficulties on inflation. Indeed, the reverse is probably true. The lack of housing starts and the fact that the supply of housing has not been growing adequately has contributed greatly to inflation. The increase in costs in the housing sector is responsible for much of the increase in the cost of living. The increase in housing costs obviously has been a major factor in workers asking for more income, which in turn brings more inflation. If we had a housing policy which worked, there would not be as much inflation in this country as there is today.
Housing starts are down 24 per cent this year. I want the minister to tell us why, if we must solve inflation by increasing supply, the supply of housing in Canada is dropping and therefore contributing to inflation. It cannot be suggested with any reality that our housing problem stems from inflation created abroad, but it may be argued that we have a serious housing problem because of the amount of inflation we have created domestically and the way we have tried to fight that inflation. Does the minister suggest that a major way to fight inflation is to raise interest rates? The government has followed this policy. High interest rates do not stem inflation. They contribute to it. Obviously, high interest rates do not slow consumer spending or capital investment, but high interest rates stop mortgage lending and the construction of apartment houses. I want the minister to tell us if he thinks you can slow down inflation by cutting down the supply of houses and whether raising interest rates will solve the problem.
The other day the minister said in the House-I do not want to misquote him-that we are moving away from boom and bust in housing in this country. We have not done that. The whole history of housing construction in Canada since 1946 shows a cyclical pattern involving high interest rates. The government follows a high interest policy and housing starts drop; it cuts down interest rates
Estimates
when the economy goes into a slump and housing starts go up. As a consequence, ever since 1946 we have had no sustained housing program.
We shall never cope with the housing problem until we eliminate this interrelationship between a monetary policy and housing. You see, all the programs the minister has put forward, in respect of which we are asked to appropriate some several hundred million dollars, will not accomplish very much at all; they will work only at the periphery of the difficuties. I support moves toward income-geared rental programs. I think we perhaps need land banks. I think we need more sewers, and so on. But these things do not really go to the heart of the issue. The real issue is whether we are to have a sustained building program which is unaffected by aberrations which may occur because of changes in general monetary policy. We have never, in this country, developed a well separated pool of funds to flow into the mortgage market, such as has been done through the building societies and savings associations in other countries. I do not know whether or not this is the answer for Canada; there are some drawbacks attached to it. But it is evident we shall never make progress until we tackle this basic issue.
The challenge to the new minister-and we all wish him great success-is to act with courage to face the fundamental issue. He must come to grips with the situation which has faced Canada ever since 1946, that is, the interrelationship between housing and general monetary policy. Does the government have any plan to partially isolate the mortgage market from the general monetary market, operating as it is? If not, no success can be expected in dealing with the housing problem as a whole. The only way in which people belonging to low income groups will ever get the housing they need lies in the industry increasing the supply of housing faster than the increase in demand over a sustained period in the metro areas. This can only happen if we devise a way of getting mortgage funds flowing into the market in a regular pattern.
I do not know whether the Minister of State for Urban Affairs wishes to adopt the same position as that taken by the Minister of Finance, namely, that inflation can be cured without causing any dislocation or trouble. No one who has studied the housing market since 1946 can help realizing that until there is some way of isolating the mortgage market more effectively we will not achieve the sustained pattern of housing construction needed to meet the needs of those living in urban areas.

better to understand this fact. If the hon. member is trying to hoodwink the people of this country, or even the members of this committee, along the lines that the government has set, or can set interest rates in isolation to reality, I think it is unfortunate. To suggest that we use it as a method of affecting the economy-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He did not suggest that.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs

Let me say this, then. We have consistently put more money into the housing market each and every year. In 1973 the figure was $923 million. In 1974 it is $1,262 million. There has been a constant pattern of increases of this nature. We have built more social housing in the past six years than was built in the previous 22 years combined. Members of the opposition ask, "Why don't you do something about it?" Evidently they were not listening when I listed 17 or 18 specific programs. When the Leader of the Opposition says we should do something about assembling land, I can only wonder where he has been. We have established a fund of half a billion dollars which is being used effectively and to which the provinces and the municipalities are responding. These are the things we are doing.
The hon. member for Don Valley raised a good point when he talked about the flow of mortgage funds. I am directing a great deal of my attention to this subject. However, I cannot come up with magical solutions because I have responsibility for taking action rather than criticizing. We must maintain the flow of these funds, but we cannot do it in isolation from world interest rates. We must do it in the real world in which we have to live. Most people recognize this fact. You cannot fool the people of Canada. Hon. members opposite could not do it in the last election, and they are not going to fool them again by this distortion of economics.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Consider what has been accomplished through the programs to which I have referred. Consider the limited dividend program. Members across the way said builders would not go along with it. But the money is there and the proposals are coming forward. We are prepared to break these funds loose. This is the way in which to use the taxpayers' dollars to the maximum advantage and break the money loose for low income housing. For the same reason, we have set up the mortgage exchange corporation. We cannot deny there is a problem, but every time there is a problem the opposition tries to turn it into a crisis. The people are not fooled by that any more. They know that life is not easy; that it is full of problems. And the government is here to deal with problems as they arise.
I feel there is a big market for investment of mortgage funds from outside this country. Many are interested in investing their money in Canada because, thanks to good government and the state of our economy, we provide a safe haven for it. I should like to see more aggressive methods used, perhaps by CMHC, to secure a greater share of this money for housing. If people abroad wish to invest a great deal of their money with financial security, they can easily find a safe investment and a productive return in this area. We will not get money into the mortgage

market unless people respond to the real world. People will not invest in that kind of situation any more than builders will build buildings when there are rent controls.
I think I have answered a few of the points that have been raised. The question of supply is fundamental. This is why, when we talk about completion of houses, the fact that we will have completed 250,000 by the end of this year-the second highest in our history-is not a bad record for a crisis situation. However, the amount that the private sector is putting into existing housing does disturb me, especially in the hon. member's beautiful city of Halifax. I would urge the private sector to put a higher ratio of their lending into new, low cost housing rather than into existing housing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the "real world" you are talking about?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, that is the real world. In the program for which I am responsible, a great percentage of the funding is going into existing housing and is doing a job, namely, helping people to buy homes. This is the kind of trade-off that we have to face. Do we use this money to help people buy homes, or for the twofold purpose of buying homes and increasing the housing stock? I made that decision knowing that it would affect people adversely, but in the belief that the ultimate benefit of all is best served by concentrating taxpayers' money into new housing. Certainly, the thrust is to increase that supply and to use it with maximum leverage to improve housing standards for Canadians.
As a matter of interest, I might mention to the hon. member for Don Valley and to the Leader of the Opposition who also spoke about supply, that there were 130,000 new family formations, 30,000 household non-family formations-a new phenomenon, I suppose, in our society- and 25,000 vacancies or losses of older homes that had deteriorated, making a total of 185,000. So the total requirement to keep up with growth amounts to 185,000 starts or completions, whichever way you wish to put it. This compares with our record last year of 268,000 starts and 250,000 starts this year.
I recognize as a valid point that there will be difficulties next year. We are down 23 per cent to 24 per cent this year, compared with our American friends who are close to 50 per cent down. So there is a problem. Nevertheless, I suggest we are doing better at controlling inflation than almost any other nation in the world, and we can do even better. Hon. members will soon hear of the new programs that I propose to introduce into the House, or modifications of existing programs from which we have learned a great deal. These will improve the situation materially.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Don Valley has a few more minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I. am astonished at the response given by the minister to the position that I have presented. Let me tell him that I am sure the people cannot be fooled all of the time. If the minister has the time, I ask him to look at the mail from his constituents who are trying to cope with the rising price of houses and
October 24, 1974

higher rents in Toronto. In view of the statements he has made, how does he account for the fact that there is such a terrific housing problem in the metropolitan area of Toronto? People do not manufacture problems. Rents are going up as never before. Prices are so high because supply is down. There is no new construction because interest rates are so high.
I hope the minister is not suggesting that the government of Canada does not influence interest rates in this country. I was trying to suggest to the minister-this is a point that he missed-that he is dead wrong if he thinks that this government has not used, either directly or indirectly, housing as a stabilizing factor on the economy. It always has, and it is doing so now.
As minister responsible for housing, should he not now be putting forth a policy or program to remove once and for all the concept that we are always going to use housing, riding on the backs of people who can least afford it, as a stabilizing factor on the economy? Obviously, interest rates are influenced by many factors, but in 1946 the government of the day was able to bring in a direct loans program which moderated the impact of general monetary policy on the mortgage market.
What I urge this new minister, a man with the respect of every member of the House, to do is try to find a way to eliminate the use of housing as a stabilizing factor. It means nothing that there will be 240,000 house completions next year, if the year after the number is going to go down and then up again like a yo-yo, always in response to monetary policy. What we need, if we are going to solve the housing problem in this country, is a well organized and well oriented construction industry that knows there is going to be a continuous flow of mortgage funds.

That is the real problem. These other considerations are just peripheral.
