speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but he was given a little extra time since the minister's reply was at some length. May I also remind the hon. member for Hamilton West that if he wants to ask a question at this point, he will be using up his time; and there are other members who rose ahead of the hon. member for Hamilton West and who should be recognized first.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very closely to the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson). To my mind, he may be going in the right direction, but the way strikes me as slightly foggy. The government has certainly done much to encourage the building of single-family units in the last few years. Still, much remains to be done.
I feel that the main problem homebuilders, private or professional, must face is that of the exorbitant cost of water and sewer mains.
In 1968, it cost $45 a linear foot to install sewers and water mains in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver. The cost has now gone up to $90 a foot in those same
Estimates
four cities. Add to that the problems created by the persisting misundertandings between the province of Quebec and the federal government.
The Quebec Department of Municipal Affairs does not decide early enough with the federal government where grants will be made for the installation of water and sewer services to allow the interested parties to pay the cost. At a cost of $90 a foot, those services are much too expensive, in the case of a 100-foot lot, for a private citizen to ever hope to own his home.
To service costs must be added the excessive interest rates, the rise in building costs over the past three years, so that for a $20,000 investment, that is, an ordinary 4-room house, the monthly payment amounts to $325, that is, $250 for mortgage and $75 for services. Once you add to this the water and school taxes, you reach a dead-end. No citizen can afford to pay $325 a month in addition to taxes for a house. He is therefore compelled to look for an apartment to rent.
In the Sherbrooke area, the situation is not so critical as elsewhere, but in such large centres as Toronto and Vancouver, where land prices have increased threefold over the past two years, it has become impossible. In these cities, people cannot build their own houses, nor avail themselves of the benefits available from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which lends low rate money to those whose annual income is less than $10,000. These people must therefore look for apartments to rent. They are willing to pay excessive rents, as in Toronto for instance.
This creates decidedly an interesting situation. Therefore, I suggest that the minister should make it possible to have better coordination between municipal, provincial and federal governments. For the sake of those who want to buy land, it should be known once and for all where the provincial government will grant subsidies to provide services.
In his contribution to the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the throne, the minister said:
So far this year CMHC has made direct loans amounting to more than $568 million to finance more than 27,000 homes-about two-thirds of them new construction. I announced a few weeks ago that we were prepared to put $50 million at 8 per cent if builders in some of the larger cities would build housing for rent at agreed-upon moderate rates.
I would point out to the minister that builders are willing to build low-cost housing. But in view of the investment cost and the lack of cooperation from municipalities which do not have the means to help them, one has to realize that the contractor has built 40-, 50- or 60-unit building whose rent he estimated at $225 or $235 a month but for which he now has to charge $300 a month because prices are changing too fast. Such a project takes six or seven months or even a year to finish. The prices have changed so much that it is impossible for the developer to rent his apartments for a reasonable price. The minister also said that:
Earlier this year we secured the co-operation of private mortgage lenders who agreed that high ratio loans should be available only for housing in the middle and lower price range.

October 24, 1974
Estimates
In my opinion, this is applicable to projects around a small town like Quebec city, Sherbrooke or Granby because, in or around those places nobody, except for a few isolated cases, thought of acquiring land and waiting until the municipality or the province decided to go ahead with development. Generally, the land was not bought by people with a view to taking advantage of the situation.
I am sure that in my area, Mr. Chairman, houses can still be built for $22,000 or $25,000. Of course, this would not be possible in Toronto or Vancouver. I had the opportunity to visit housing projects in Toronto, big construction projects for what was supposed to be moderately priced housing, but actually the apartments are renting out at $300 or $400 a month. This housing was built for people whose income is less than $12,000 a year. They just cannot afford them. The builders keep them empty for one or two years or often go bankrupt, and the CMHC only has a small amount to pay and has to have houses finished in order for them to have some sort of value.
If the minister has low cost housing in mind, he still has a long way to go in the future to manage it. The minister also told us that the government will establish for next year, as it did last year, a general classification for people who buy a moderately priced house for the first time. They have suggested that a $500 subsidy be granted as a form of compensation to those who are particularly in need of help to pay sales taxes on building materials. That matter was dealt with in the last estimates and I think that suggestion will be put forward again as soon as it can possibly be.
I urge the minister to go on in that way, but I think the $500 subsidy which would lower the cost of buying a house should be raised to $1,000. Most of all, the CMHC should ensure that the subsidy would really be used to buy the house. It would otherwise profit the contractor or the intermediaries.
I think the minister seems to go in the right direction, and I believe that this amount of $500 should be paid to the home buyer.
Mr. Chairman, the minister has also announced that he would relieve of a part of his income tax the buyer of a first house, whether it be a young couple or the individual who buys a single family home for the first time. I did not go thoroughly into his speech and I do not know whether the matter concerns only a single family home or a duplex, but I think it is the former. If his intention is such, I am convinced that we will pass a worthy legislation. That could contribute to relieve the congestion of large cities, and eventually allow everybody to own a house.
Mr. Chairman, there is another matter I would like to bring to the minister's attention. It concerns the scale used in respect of the salary which must be earned by the individual who wants to get a mortgage loan at a low interest rate.
Anyone who now earns less than $7,400 a year is not entitled to the annual $500 grant. I would like to suggest to the minister to increase the grant to $1,000 a year since, at the present time, according to the established scale, the person who really needs a house and supports a small family is generally the one who earns the lowest salary. Those who earn high annual salaries of $20,000 or $25,000 do not worry at all because they can easily buy a house.

On the other hand, for the one whose annual income ranges from $5,500 to $8,000, there is a difference of $2,000 which should be taken into consideration by the minister.
The minister said later that the year 1975 would be fruitful for the low wage earner who will want to acquire a house. As for me, I am not as optimistic as the minister, because I believe that the rate of interest must stop increasing or stay at the present level for at least one year.
On the basis of my personal experience, I can say that in 1974 my company built houses at an interest rate of 93A, 10 M and 11 Vi per cent. This is a significant change if we think about a $19,000 mortgage on a single family dwelling. It makes all the difference, and, finally, the person who was interested yesterday in buying a house will not be able to afford it tomorrow, because his salary will not have changed while his obligations and purchasing power will.
I believe that the minister would be making some progress if he could tell us when the interest rates of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will stop changing every three, four or six months and will finally be stabilized. In my opinion, this would be helpful.
I would also like to point out to the minister that to set the construction industry back on its feet, or at least to maintain it, it is essential that the person in charge of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation meet more often with the Minister of Municipal Affairs of each province so that cities can develop harmoniously. More land should also be made available to those who want to build a house.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. We are now engaged in a debate involving individual members, but perhaps the House will bear with me for a moment. I have not heard the minister say one word about senior citizens. With all due respect, I think this is one of the most important aspects of the housing industry. I know the minister receives letters, just as other members do. I remember during the election, as I am sure the minister does, knocking on the doors of senior citizens on the third floor of buildings. I want to know what effort is being made by the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities working together to relieve this very serious situation.
Ever since I have been here the situation has been that the supply is nowhere near the demand. I want to know what we can expect from this department to give some relief to our senior citizens. I heard the minister emphasize the young and the middle-aged. I go along with him to a point, but I think the priority should be in terms of the senior citizens. What is his department doing in respect of this very serious problem?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has heard me speak about the young and the middle-aged. I think it is important that we be concerned about everyone. I believe my hon. friend has also heard me speak
October 24, 1974

about my personal priority in the social field, which happens to relate to senior citizens. Because I do not wish to create any false hopes, build up expectations or play a game with the senior citizens, to whom we have great responsibility and for whom we have great respect, I want to make certain that I have the exact figures so that I may be specific. There are many programs involving the municipalities and the provinces. There is the limited dividend program. Some are non-profit programs and some are co-operative programs.
They are not working, and you know it.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: I want to make sure that I give the hon. member and the senior citizens an accurate answer in this regard. I hope the hon. gentleman will bear with me, and perhaps at the next opportunity to intervene I will give these figures precisely. I think, in all fairness, there have been improvements in some constituencies. Many members from all sides of the House have spoken to me about senior citizens' housing and are aware of the responses that have been made. There have been improvements; it is almost a minor miracle. I am not saying, however, that we have solved the problem. If the hon. member wishes to play games, that is up to him, but I intend to give an honest answer.

On a question of privilege, as a member of the class of '68 I am a little surprised at the minister. At no time have I implied that I was playing games. I am shocked to think that the minister would look at the hon. member for Hamilton West and think he is playing games in this important area. He may talk about other constituencies, but I know that in Hamilton West, if I do not receive three or four letters a week from senior citizens in this regard, something is wrong. The supply is not there. It does not look as if the situation is changing at all. The situation may be different in some other constituency. But I want to know whether these people can expect relief. It is a shame that they should have to live in this standard of housing. The minister knows this as well as I do. He should not be bombastic about this problem.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. With all due respect to the hon. member for Hamilton West, I must remind him that he took the floor first on a point of order and next on a question of privilege. I do not believe that in fact he had a point of order or a question of privilege; he rose to intervene in the debate. That would be acceptable except for the fact that the Chair had recognized another member of his party. If that hon. member is prepared to yield to the hon. member for Hamilton West, then the hon. member for Hamilton West may proceed.
I so yield, Mr. Chairman.
Mr. Chairman, I certainly accept the remonstrance given me and I shall now sit down, because I know I have made the point with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on another point of order. Since this question was raised on a point of order, I would like to answer it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. It is not a point of order at all. The minister is rising to speak to a point of
Estimates
order which was not, in fact, a point of order under the rules. At the next opportunity the minister has to rise, he may incorporate the answer in his remarks. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the urban affairs estimates I wish to devote my time to Canada's housing problems and the need to assist Canadians in obtaining decent shelter at reasonable cost. It is a time for action, not reports, studies and statistics like the $100 million urban demonstration program that the Liberal government proposed last March. This $100 million study is nothing but a diversionary tactic and is clearly ineffective to assist in solving the existing housing crisis. The $100 million could be spent much more wisely, such as in providing serviced lots and reducing interest rates.
To say there is a national housing crisis in Canada is the understatement of the century. Housing costs are rising at a rapid rate. We must now look to new programs and approaches to provide more housing, and more economical housing. One area to which we must give careful consideration is the provision of more mobile homes and trailer parks. Mobile homes can be made permanent as they are a kind of prefabricated housing. Today I wish to present a new horizon for housing, namely, satellite towns and attractive residential parks. The popularity of mobile homes is increasing steadily. An estimated 25,000 new units were used in 1972 in Canada. More people are turning to mobile homes than to other more conventional types of residences.
Today I will speak of a more community-oriented type of mobile home area, with proper fire protection and facilities. Today, the lifetime family home has all but disappeared due to a wide variety of social and economic causes. People move about with mounting frequency. This factor of mobility in modern family life has reached the point where it warrants due consideration in every urban study. I should like to quote from a recent news release entitled "Canadian families are moving more". It reads:
More Canadian families moved from one city to another last year than in 1972, says the Coast to Coast Real Estate Service.
A survey of long distance moves shows that 21,777 households were relocated in another city during 1973 compared with 17,493 a year earlier.
More than half the trips originated in Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa, about 20 per cent in Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver and 10 per cent in Halifax and Quebec city. The balance of the long distance transfer business was shared by other major urban centres such as Hamilton, Regina, Saskatoon and Victoria.
Coast to Coast Real Estate Service is an association of more than 100 realtors in 187 offices across Canada.
Frank Hodges, vice-president and manager of corporate relations for A. E. LePage Limited, Toronto, a real estate company, said recently nearly 750,000 families changed their place of residence last year, the vast majority within the same city or to nearby communities in the same province.
If the trend in the mobility rate, as indicated by family allowance statistics, continues, he said, Canadian families a few years from now will be moving once every three years.
"Being moved has become a way of life for certain occupations", he said. "Our own experience would seem to show that the number of household relocations is evenly split between government departments and agencies and private business".

October 24, 1974
Estimates
A typical case is that of a head of family transferred by his company to another city. Commonly, the wife and family stay behind until the house is sold and the current school term is finished. Houses take time to sell. As the holiday time draws near, the wife becomes increasingly anxious to sell. Far too often it happens that in order to resolve the long uncertainty and rejoin her husband, she takes a beating on the sale. At the other end, the husband is unfamiliar with the prices of houses in the city to which he has moved. He also has a deadline in the purchase of a home, and it is quite possible for him also to take a beating on the price he agrees to pay. At both ends someone pays a substantial real estate commission. Excellent jobs in faraway places are constantly presented by Manpower, but they are often beyond the reach of the man who owns his home. This type of situation works to the disadvantage of both employer and employee.
Circumstances such as these, together with the rising cost of houses, have created booming trailer sales across the country. But trailers have their limitations. In many ways they are a poor substitute for a conventional home. But the market continues to expend and where sufficient need exists, development will follow. It may well be that mobile homes will evolve in ways that have not yet been considered. A possibility with a seemingly great potential is that of a combination of the old and the new. Why not have basic mobile units with supplemental stationary living space available, on a rental basis, in designated residential areas in every major population centre of the country?
The two sections of the mobile home would be readily attachable. This is the only part of either unit that would need to be standard. The mobile unit is not too large, as trailer sizes go, but it is completely self-contained. It would make a practical, low-cost home for several years for a newly married couple. Any time they wish, they can obtain a supplementary unit on a rental basis, and if and when they want to move all they have to do is move their furniture out of the rental unit into their mobile home and they are ready to go. They can turn their mobile unit progressively into a two, three or four-bedroom house complete with basement, in any part of the country, as the family's needs expand, and when the children have grown up and moved away the parents are not faced with the costly problem of disposing of a house that has become too large for their needs. They can go back to their original trailer unit and in retirement or old age move anywhere they wish.
This type of combination unit lends itself to satellite towns, slum clearance projects, new mining towns in out-of-the-way places, and especially to armed forces personnel. Both the supplementary and the mobile unit are within a wide price range, and also there is a wide choice in the type of lot on which they can be located. Spacious lots with lawns and gardens, or modest lots at a minimum price may be available. A sufficient number of lots would have to be available for unattached trailers as well as combination units. Mobile units will have to be somewhat wider than highway regulations now permit, but if the need arises both the legislation and the highways will adjust.

There is an opportunity for radical change in both the design and methods of construction of mobile units. Not only the mobile unit, but the relatively small and simple stationary section could be built in a centrally located factory on a mass-production basis and easily moved to the desired location. The plumbing facilities will all be in the mobile unit, the heating will be electric, with the panel located in the mobile unit. The mobile unit will tend to become more like a conventional house and less like the present type of trailer.
The wheels could be eliminated and the chassis redesigned in such a way as to allow for ready transportation on a low-bed unit. The present practice is to move the trailer with a rented tractor, so why not have the tractor supply the wheels also and carry the mobile unit instead of pulling it? This would save a great many sets of wheels which are seldom used and it would reduce construction costs. The mobile unit will have to be placed on some type of surface foundation with a heated crawl-space. It will have to be sufficiently light and rigid to lend itself to moving.
The mobile unit plan I propose takes up an area of 488 square feet. The construction cost of conventional homes today is approximately $22 or more per square foot, exclusive of the price of the lot. At that price, the cost of a dwelling of this size would be approximately $9,900. This price, however, includes a basement, installed sewer and water lines, and municipal fees, which altogether would amount to at least $2,800. This would reduce the cost to $7,100. Add $300 to this price for selling costs, and we have a round figure of $7,400. With the economy of large-scale, mass-production methods, this is a realistic figure. With a down payment of $500 and a subsidized rate of 8 per cent, a monthly payment of $78.87 would pay off the balance owing in 12 years. The three-bedroom supplementary rental unit has 390 square feet of floor space. At $20 per square foot, construction costs will amount to $7,800. This figure includes complete plumbing and kitchen and bathroom cabinetwork, but these are in the mobile unit. The control panel for the electrical heating and lighting is also located in the mobile unit. There is also the factor of centralized mass-production methods of construction. Altogether, the saving per square foot could amount to as much as $2,600. Building lots in developments specifically designed for the purpose, beyond the scope of the land speculators, might start at a minimum price of $2,500, with larger and more expensive lots available. We thus arrive at a minimum cost of approximately $7,700.
If the residential park is owned by a Crown corporation and operated on a non-profit basis, the basic cost to the tenant would be taxes, interest on the investment, depreciation and administration. Interest at 8 per cent on $7,700 amounts to $56 per month. Taxes on a dwelling of this value should not run over $25 per month. Let us say a minimum rental of $85 per month for the three-bedroom unit, with four bedrooms costing a little more and two bedrooms a little less. The rent on parking space for the trailer alone would run from $5 per month up, depending upon the area required and the number, if any, of school-age children. It thus appears that payments on the mobile
October 24, 1974

unit, plus the rental on a supplementary unit, could be held to a minimum of $110 per month.
In the time it would take for a newly married couple to reach the point where a supplementary unit became necessary, the monthly payment could be held to a minimum of $55 to $60. With the addition of the supplementary rental unit, the price would go up to $110, where it would remain until the mobile unit was paid for, at which time it would drop back to the $65, more or less, rental for the supplementary unit. When the children grew up and moved away, the rent could be reduced to the price of a parking lot for the mobile unit alone on the basis of a childless couple, perhaps not over $10 per month.
This is a housing concept of a truly revolutionary nature. It may have sufficient merit to become a major factor in the building industry. Five hundred residential parks, with an average capacity of 1,000 dwellings, including both single and combination units, might not be too much to look for in the first five or six years of operation. The provision of so many low-cost homes of this type could not fail to have a profound effect upon all other types of housing. It would have a powerful effect upon the currently inflated prices obtainable for every type of older home.
The type of residential development required could be designed to be aesthetically acceptable. There would be trees and lawns and boulevards and playgrounds for the children, as in any modern suburb. In every case, the supplementary unit would be in front and the mobile unit hidden from view at the rear. In the residential parks, there also could be variations in exterior design. Many variations and improvements would be sure to follow if the project is put into operation.
No doubt there will be criticism of my proposal, but I hope it is constructive and perhaps others will have new ideas and innovations to put forward. But mainly, we must take drastic measures to lower housing costs. I believe my satellite town proposal is a step in the right direction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to begin by congratulating the minister on the portfolio which he now holds. When he and I came to this House in 1968, we were seatmates. I did not think he would go so far to get away from me. I was interested to hear the hon. member for Don Valley and the Leader of the Opposition refer to the minister as affable and say that he was seemingly trying to smile away his problems. I would suggest to them that they not underestimate the tenacity and competitiveness of the minister. They should not be misled by his affability or smile, because the minister has a very enviable war record. He came through the war and established a business, making a huge success of it. He has fought three successful election campaigns and now sits on the treasury benches. All this should be an indication of the toughness and tenacity of the minister. I would say, if they need to be reminded on the other side, that they should speak to the gentleman who spent almost a quarter of a million dollars in two elections trying to take the seat away from the minister.

Let's get into the housing problem.
Estimates

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Hamilton West thought the only way he could get into this debate was by bootlegging a point of order and a question of privilege. He indicated his concern for social housing, and I know he has that concern.
You betcha.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The problem is that when his party was in power, unhappily they did not have that concern. Can you imagine how many senior citizen housing units we would have today if they had come up with the idea in 1957-58? Now we have to catch up because of the failure of that party.
Mr. Chairman, I, too, was sitting as a backbencher and considering the AHOP program and listening to the opposition's criticism that it would never be used. Not only is it working, but funds are running out and in some areas they ran out because of its success. I think the former minister is to be congratulated for this and I hope the present minister will be successful in obtaining more funds for the program.
The members who have addressed the committee today, Mr. Chairman, have been mainly from our larger centres, such as Halifax, Don Valley, Toronto, Broadview, Vancouver and Hamilton West-with his bootleg comment.
That's all right. I made my point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We have not heard as much from the smaller areas and I should like to make a representation on behalf of the Sarnia-Lambton area. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent is not present, but I know he shares my concern over the impact of the expansion of the petrochemical industry in the Sarnia-Lambton area. There is going to be a desperate need for housing there.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has suggested a program. Perhaps that is the way we will have to handle the problem of many people moving into a particular area, because of construction, who will ultimately leave the area. That is the kind of positive response that I like to hear from members of the opposition; not just criticism but positive suggestions. I do not know whether the hon. member's idea has merit, but I think it warrants study.
The mayor of Sarnia has written to the minister on behalf of the city and its environs, indicating that in the next five or six years 6,000 or 7,000 people will be in the area at one time. This is a matter of serious concern, not so much to the city of Sarnia but to the townships, because there is no more room to build within the city boundaries. The township have the problem of becoming dormitories only, because they have to rely on a real estate tax base that has not much industry. This problem should be resolved by the federal government, the provincial government and the municipal governments working in co-operation.
I am happy that the deputy minister of housing for the province of Ontario met with the mayor of Sarnia. They have announced that there will be an area housing study. I would ask the minister to give consideration to lending some personnel from his department to participate in this study. The minister speaks primarily of ten critical market

October 24, 1974
Estimates
areas, but it seems to me that one more should be added- the Sarnia-Lambton area. I do not think municipalities can handle a problem of this scope, because they do not have the tax money available. It should not be left entirely to the provinces, either. This is a situation where the three levels of government should get together.
Why are we so sensitive about this problem, Mr. Chairman. People in the Sarnia area remember when the Polymer Corporation moved in during the war; they remember the emergency that resulted from the construction which took place. There was an influx of people and we ended up with a section of the community called Blue Water. Houses were just thrown up. Then 15 or 20 years ago we had the expense of clearing out that area, expropriating and compensating people for their substandard homes and moving them to other parts of the city.
There is a little time left, and we want to avoid problems. Therefore, I hope the minister will consider the representations of the mayor which were set out in a letter he wrote the minister and the Minister of Finance. This project concerns an area larger than Sarnia. If the kind of expansion Alberta is embarking upon takes place, such a program could form a pilot project which could affect people who are required to move out of an area once construction work has ceased. I think in this way light could be shed on how to cope with a serious problem.

Mr. Chairman, I join my colleagues in congratulating the minister upon his appointment, and wish him well. Considering the poor act he is following, he cannot help but look good. From what the minister said in the House and in committee, one would think there is no housing problem, that talk of slums and inadequate housing is nothing more than a rumour started by 200,000 or
300,000	Canadians who live in substandard houses. Some of the programs the minister announced are not performing the function intended for them. With all these intials, NIP, LIP, LEAP, AHOP, and so on, I expect that in ten years we shall have a third official language in Canada.
The neighbourhood Improvement Program is not working as well as it should. It discriminates against the poor provinces because, although the government agrees to make funds available under the program, the balance must be made up by the municipality or province, which may not be financially capable of providing the required equity. For example, under the Neighbourhood Improvement Program, the government gives as a grant 50 per cent of the cost of a project and lends 75 per cent of the rest. This must be paid back by the municipality, and the province must also come up with a substantial amount of equity. It is no use providing, say, $.5 million to St. John's, a city of which I can speak with some authority, because the city cannot match the government's offer and cannot undertake the program.
What is the minister's motive in restricting assisted home ownership for new houses? I suggest the reasons given by him justify a continuation of the application of the program in the purchase of older houses. Not everybody who can qualify for AHOP can afford or wants to buy a new house. I suppose the minister thinks that if AHOP applies to new housing, it will boost the building
(Mr. Cullen.]
industry and result in increased starts and completions. Obviously, his plan is failing. In September of this year housing starts were 34 per cent below those of the previous year. The program is not proving effective in providing new homes, and the results are apparent with the lumber industry and with trades connected with the building industry.
I join my colleague from Hamilton West in saying that we must treat our citizens more fairly. Like the hon. member, I have received many inquiries from senior citizens in my constituency who have begged me to intercede on their behalf and find for them a decent place in which they can live their last few years. Is it not a sad commentary on our government and on our society that our senior people who gave so much in the service of this country, who raised families and contributed so much to the development of this country, should spend their last few years pinching pennies, trying to make ends meet, and often paying rents which are totally unacceptable, considering their meagre incomes. In many cases their only source of income is their old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement.
I draw the minister's attention to the situation existing in my riding. I suspect the same conditions prevail elsewhere in Canada. I am talking about the raw deal we have given our senior citizens. Some senior citizens' apartments are in complexes that were built under the limited dividend section of the act-section 16, I believe. I think the minister is familiar with this question. I gave him copies of letters which I had sent to his predecessor. It turns out that the occupants of these homes are now in their sixties and seventies and are not eligible for government assistance or subsidy to offset the increasingly high rents they must pay. I suggest the government must help old people living in these complexes to qualify for some type of assistance, some type of subsidy similar to that given to people in apartments which were built under section 44 of the National Housing Act. Under that section, the federal government provides 50 per cent of the subsidy and the province and municipality the other 50 per cent.
I want the minister to tell us what steps are being taken to alleviate the harsh burden being carried by so many of our senior citizens. I have evidence that the people who live in these homes-which, by the way, were built through public financing under the limited dividend section of the act-are paying as much as 70 per cent of their total income in rent. This makes a mockery of the income formula which has been adopted by the government and by CMHC and has been used by them in computing mortgage payments, and so on. A further interesting aspect is this that one of the conditions under which these apartments were built is as follows:
The rentals to be charged shall be rentals which the corporation deems to be fair and reasonable having regard to the probable family income of the occupants of each family housing unit.
So I contend that the government has a serious responsibility to the people who occupy homes which were built under that section of the National Housing Act, a solemn responsibility to ensure that the rents being charged are fair and reasonable and bear a reasonable relationship to the family income of those occupying the units. I could
October 24, 1974

continue, but there is not much I can say that has not already been said in the course of this debate. I wish to impress upon the minister the importance of doing something for our senior citizens. speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
In view of the concern expressed by the hon. member for Hamilton West and by the hon. member for St. John's West, I think the committee might be interested in figures relating to senior citizens' housing. None of us would ever agree that we have enough, but out of a $400 million budget for non-profit housing over 50 per cent goes to senior citizens. That is a bias in favour of senior citizens by comparison with the rest of the population.
Moreover, in the public housing sector of the senior citizens' housing program the existing stock totals 32,895. Currently under construction across Canada are 16,400 units. So the stock presently under construction represents an increase of almost 50 per cent. This is being done in accordance with programs which hon. members opposite find inadequate. I agree they are inadequate.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: I should like to double that number, or triple it. We talk of problems, and there are problems. But we are meeting them head on. And this does not include the non-profit housing, in which sector another 6,000 units came on this year, that is between January and September.
And the people are still waiting for houses.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Well, I expect some rational approach from hon. members opposite. We would like to do everything at one time, but even Liberals cannot do that. I am not satisfied. We want to do more. I see the hon. member for Hamilton West has just returned to the chamber. I am sure he heard the figures from behind the curtain. I have been very impressed by the quality of the debate this afternoon. Hon. members have referred to me as being affable and smiling. That is one of my problems. I refuse to carry the world on my back as a burden, but I take my job deadly seriously. I always have. Whatever I have accomplished in life has been through working extremely hard and never giving in.
True to the class of '68.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
The important thing is not to take oneself too seriously. I see a lot of people here who take themselves so deadly seriously that it is frightening. But they do not accomplish anything. However, as hon. members pointed out, we do have problems. Some of them are being managed quite well, though there are others which perhaps are not being managed to our own satisfaction. We

have made mistakes, but they have been mistakes of comission. We have some excellent programs in force now.
We have been talking here-some will say ad nauseam- about AHOP. The fact is that AHOP has been very highly successful, and since it has been so successful I want to find out whether we can stretch it still further, even though it may not be perfect. As to limited dividend rental housing, it is important for us to realize that the rental housing situation is probably the closest thing approaching a crisis which confronts us unless we fail to act quickly, particularly in the major centres.
That is exactly what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: This is why we have used a section of the National Housing Act, section 15, in order to secure funds which would normally have been used in other programs-programs which for one reason or another were not moving quickly. So we found $50 million for the last quarter of this year. Everyone said it could not be done, that nobody would respond. Well, they are responding right across the country. Sixteen developers have shown interest in St. John's, Newfoundland, alone, and 53 in Toronto alone. Yet the hon. member for Broadview was saying, I believe, that these were unrealistic levels. They were unrealistic, he said, because no one could buy a house at that price at that time. What has happened? I have the figure here of the number of AHOP units built in Toronto. It is 1,080. The fact is the price of housing was not related to costs, and when we provided money to purchase houses they were available at those prices. This is what we are achieving, and this is the success we intend to exploit.
That is like giving a peanut to a starving elephant.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member were to go to areas of the country in which his party's policies were in force, and saw what is happening there, he might not be too enamored, though I must say some of the provinces have taken great advantage of federal funding for limited dividend and senior citizens programs, and so on. I regret, sometimes, that it is not quite clear where this money is coming from.
Answer the question put to you.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am aware of the problem to which the hon. member has alluded, and it does disturb me. There is an inequity here. Although programs are improved as they go along, people who took advantage of a program which seemed very attractive at the time are now finding them less attractive than newer programs. I cannot promise anything definite. In some respects this problem is in the same category as perpetual bonds, old annuities. When do you start making them retroactive? But I recognize the problem. It is something we must look into, perhaps in conjunction with my provincial counterparts, to find ways to make the programs more equitable so they assist these people.

One final, short question, Mr. Chairman. In view of the fact that these apartments are financed by the federal government under the National Housing Act, would the minister undertake to commence consultation with his provincial counterparts-I ask this question because the federal government has a vested interest in these apartments-with a view to working out some kind of arrangement under which people living in such apartments will qualify for a subsidy which will bring their rents down, hopefully, to an acceptable amount?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: I understand the hon. member's concern. We are presently in touch with the provincial authorities. Some programs apply to fixed rents, older ones to low rents. Others are geared to income. But the whole subject is under review. I assure the hon. member it is a problem I take seriously, and I shall take a special interest in these consultations.

Mr. Chairman, I could not help listening with wonderment to the glowing words of the minister in charge of housing. Last year we built about 280,000 houses, and ministers of the government at that time were very

proud of that number. This year, although we are down 25 per cent from that number, they are still proud and are still boasting, even though there is no evidence at all that we have come anywhere near to meeting the needs of the people of Canada. There is no reason for the decline in housing starts except for the fact that the price of building a house and the interest rate at which houses have to be financed have risen to the extent that people cannot afford to purchase a home.
One of our criticisms of the AHOP program of which the minister is so proud is that it is insufficiently funded. The minister always tries to deny that fact, yet today he has told the committee that 1,000 homes, approximately, have been financed under the AHOP program in the city of Toronto-1,000 homes in a metropolitan area now populated by about two million people! Surely even this government recognizes how far short of meeting our housing needs this program falls.
People want to buy houses, but the cannot afford them. The minister ignores the fact that in many countries, including the United States to the south of us, governments have instructed banks and mortgage companies to lend money for mortgage purposes at regulated rates substantially lower than the commercial rate. I am not sure what the rate is in the United States at the present time, but it is substantially less than the 12 Vi to 13 per cent people in Canada pay. Countries such as Sweden and many western European countries have similar programs.
Thousands of families in this country cannot afford, and are not likely ever to be able to afford, a home. Thousands of our native people are without adequate shelter. It has been estimated that there are 10,000 Indian families who need new homes right now, but there is no program to meet their need. Large numbers of native people move into cities, particularly in western Canada-Winnipeg, Regina, Calgary and Vancouver-and even if they have a skill, they cannot find a job and do not have even the smallest of down payments under any program of the Canadian government that assists people to purchase a home.
What these people need is rental housing. The minister says we are building a substantial number of units, but this is like telling a person who wants to buy a bicycle that there are no bicycles but lots of Cadillacs being built, so he should buy a Cadillac. It was once said of the people of France that all citizens were equal and had the right to sleep under a bridge over the Seine, and this is what the minister is saying to those who are looking for housing. Just whom are we building houses for? Would the minister tell us when we are going to start meeting the needs of the people of Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal who are living in dilapidated houses, houses that simply do not meet the standards of a country as wealthy as Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member asking me a question?

Before I get off the subject of housing, would the minister explain what he is doing about the

reorganization of his department? speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Eighty-five per cent.
Someone suggests 85 per cent. However, the exact figure is not important.
And that is sad.

It may be sad, but it is a fact of life. I should like to know whether the minister and his department are really looking at the problems that will flow from this urban growth. What are the minister and his department doing about developing land? Let me give two illustrations-and I do not want to get into the same bind I got into last night with the Minister of Transport. I will refer to the metropolitan Toronto and metropolitan Montreal areas. Another airport in the Montreal area has already been started at Mirabel. In the not too distant future another airport will be constructed in the Toronto area. The estimated cost of providing rapid transit from the new Montreal airport is $450 million. I am not aware of what it will cost to provide rapid transit to the Pickering airport, but I am certain it will be as much if not more.
Following the construction of a new airport, we find new factories, new housing developments and new commercial developments. Is the minister's department involved with the provincial and municipal governments in planning ahead for these things, or will we wake up one morning with a new airport at Mirabel, only to find it takes two hours to fly from Montreal to Winnipeg but two hours to get from the airport to downtown Montreal, and the same situation at Pickering? I should like the minister to deal with that problem.
What role is the minister's department playing in the movement of railway terminals from their present locations in the major cities, with all their assets, to new locations? Are we going to allow the CPR and the CNR, which is theoretically a publicly-owned corporation, to move from their present locations, as they did in Montreal, to new locations, selling their present locations, incuding yards and stations which are often extremely valuable properties, to the highest bidder in order to obtain as much money as possible?
That is what happened in Montreal. Tens of thousands of people were then brought into the area without any

consideration given to how they were to be transported. Is the minister's department, the Department of Transport, the Department of the Environment, or any federal department going to get in on the ground floor in advance of these developments to see that things are done according to an orderly plan which will meet the social and economic needs of the people in the areas, or are we to permit these grandiose developments without the benefit of order, as we have in past years?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
To answer the specific question, I should mention that I was in the hon. member's city last Monday and met with the distinguished mayor-who I presume was re-elected yesterday-and the premier of the province. As to what we are doing in that city under the Neighbourhood Improvement Program, let me remind the hon. member of the Selkirk Park project involving a commitment of over $4 million; the Midland housing project, which I understand is to involve another $2 million, along with the cultural centre which is to cost some $600,000. In so far as housing starts are concerned, I can only repeat again what is being done under AHOP. There are 900 units being built in metropolitan Winnipeg. That should not be related to what is being done in Toronto because one must realize that many of the housing starts in Toronto are not really within the metropolitan area.
In this group which is being served, the average family income is $6,852 per annum, with some 30 per cent having a family income of less than $6,000. Those are figures that apply across Canada and I think that is a pretty good indication that we are serving the right people. I am delighted that the member has raised these questions. I was also interested in the hon. member's comment about providing Cadillacs to people who are riding bicycles. But it is interesting to note that when money is available at low cost, housing starts increase. Having regard to urban policy, I am deeply involved and interested in such a policy relating to housing per se for individual communities. This is still a very active policy on the part of CMHC, requiring a great deal of intergovernmental coordination on a trilevel basis. The ministry itself is actively interested in this area.
The hon. member raised an interesting question regarding the Mirabel airport. The construction of such an airport has a major influence on urban development, particularly in the case of the largest city in Canada. It involves
80,000	acres under federal control. There is what is known as the Tram study specifically in relation to a transportation plan such as the hon. member mentions. I believe Mr. Douglas Fullerton is chairing that committee for the province of Quebec. Our representative is Mr. Douglas Ryan, a senior member of the ministry. So we are actively involved. This is a perfect example of co-ordination in these areas of government. These people are extremely interested in transportation.
When you think of the amount of planning required in respect of major transportation systems, such as the one between the Mirabel airport and downtown Montreal, and the acreage involved, you can imagine the amount of urban planning that must take place at three levels of government. This is of tremendous importance and I am sure these people are working seriously on the problem. The question of railway relocations is under active con-

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Madam Chairman, the projects of which I am aware in Winnipeg relating to the native people are Camew and Neeginan. It is a problem which I know the premier has taken seriously. This is a problem which he spoke about to me and my colleagues. It is an area I should like to explore further. It is of particular interest. I think the problems are rather serious. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps hon. members will pardon my interruption. In view of the very limited time remaining, in respect of this department, between now and five o'clock, perhaps it would be the desire of hon. members to limit themselves to question and answers of the minister. Is that agreed?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We will do our best.
Agreed.

Madam Chairman, since you are so agreeable I will go along with you on this. I have just a few points which I shall put in the form of questions and, hopefully, the minister will do his best to answer them. First of all, following the subject raised by my colleagues in respect of senior citizens' housing, the minister indicated that another 6,000 units were in the process of being built. I wonder whether consideration is being given, in the design of senior citizens' homes under the non-profit sector, to providing for people who are disabled and physically handicapped. I could dwell on this matter for many moments. I wonder whether the minister would ask his officials if consideration is being given to this matter, or what their plans are.
The minister indicated that in order to meet the need,
185,000	homes are required. Those provided over the past two or three years and this year represent a quarter of a million. I wonder whether the minister is aware of the increasing need because of the baby boom since World War II and DREE incentive grants which have caused expansion in places that were not industrialized before, thus creating the movement of people such as technicians and others in specialty trades. It would seem that because of this situation some infrastructure should be provided beyond the 250,000 homes, in order to cope with the problem.
If I might be a little parochial, I wish to say that through the investment of DREE funds, the district I represent on the west coast of Newfoundland is in the process of spending hundreds of millions of dollars to bring power across from Labrador to Newfoundland by way of cable. This is an isolated area and because of the jobs created there will be a need for water and sewage services as well as housing, because many people will have to move there.
Then moving down my coast, just recently a zinc mine was started which employs 300 people. This situation should also be taken into consideration. A program should be developed through DREE to work out a solution to these problems and to ensure that the money is found for places where it is needed. I could point out places where the minister could find $100 million.
I did not listen to the first speaker, so perhaps this question has been answered, but under the urban demonstration program I understand there is $100 million allocated. I do not think this is required. I wonder if the minister would consider taking this $100 million and transferring it to programs such as AHOP, NIP and RRAP. The other thing on which the minister might comment concerns the $100 million rural native housing program. This program would fulfil a great need in rural Canada, particularly in rural Newfoundland. In the release of the

minister's predecessor I believe it was suggested that 100,000 homes should be built for rural and native people over the next five years. There are not too many native people in my area, although there are many rural people who do not have the necessary funds to build homes.
Another way in which I suggest the minister could save money to help overcome the emergency would be to expand the $10 million NIP and RRAP programs. I am sure there are thousands of substandard homes in Canada. Many of these people wish to build new homes. I should like the minister to give us an indication of his relationship with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in providing housing to support industry, and also his relationship with the Minister of Veterans Affairs in respect of overcoming the housing needs of veterans who cannot acquire homes through the limited funds available under part II of the act.
I would dwell now on another matter. I have been talking to a person from Corner Brook. A university is being built there. I was told that in order to provide homes for students, the cost of the land involved would be $18,000. I am not talking about Toronto or Montreal but about Newfoundland. This is the amount required to provide a serviced lot for the many students who would be coming into this medium-sized city. In order to allow other members to have an opportunity to speak, I will leave those questions with the minister and hope he will reply to them.

The Minister of Veterans Affairs and myself have a very close relationship and we have been having discussions. We happen, both of us, to be veterans. I have to be careful with my words now. At one time no one listened to me, but now I have to be careful of what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Some of the programs which we veterans honestly and in our hearts understand were designed for us when we were young veterans after the war and are not applicable now. I should like to put a couple of questions to the minister. One refers to a matter he raised in his speech in reply to an hon. member, namely, that he wants people in the constituencies to know that federal funds are being made available. speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I am already working on procedures that will be automatic and will involve the local member, because we all have an interest in showing the federal presence. Would the minister like to respond to this attitude of people in towns of less than 10,000?

speechtext: NHA guarantees are applicable. There are some very remote areas where private lenders will not service such loans; we move in as lenders of last resort in such situations. But as regards smaller communities, if we are not being active and are not serving a purpose, I wish the hon. member would provide me or the corporation with the information. However, I do not think that that is often the case.
Is it not a fact that CMHC will not assist with mortgages where there are no sewage facilities?

speechtext: The proper answer is that it is not a fact in the sense that we do assist where no sewage facilities are available in the normal trunk services. But we do have a sewage tank policy.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Where the installation meets certain standards, where the size of the lot is adequate and meets local standards, this is the case. We are trying to avoid strip development. I have a rather long speech, Madam Chairman, but I think I will put my questions to the minister one at a time. They are very short. The first question involves interest on first mortgages. I have had a question on the order paper for a long time asking whether the government has figures as to cost if we were to allow people to deduct interest on their first mortgages from income before calculating taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, I have not seen the question. I do try to answer those questions as rapidly as possible. This would be more properly a question for the Minister of Finance. It is one of the options at which the minister responsible for housing must look at all times. There are obvious inequities and obvious benefits in the situation. We see it happening in other jurisdictions. All I can say is that I look at this as one of the options with less priority.

My second question involves the 11 per cent federal sales tax. Again, I have had this question on the order paper for a long time. Can government officials figure out what it would cost the government of Canada if the 11 per cent sales tax was removed? The first and second questions involve the Minister of Finance, but I think this is important policy which should be looked into by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. Whether or not he agrees with the policy-this is certainly the policy in other countries of the free western world-it is a matter that should be looked into. I wonder if the minister's officials have figured out how much it would cost the country to eliminate the 11 per cent sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: On dwellings it would be somewhere in the area of $450 million to $500 million. Taking it off all building materials, the figure would be well in excess of $1 billion which would have to be compensated.

My final question concerns the 1 per cent premium that is charged on total loans as mortgage insurance which is held in trust and managed by CMHC. I am wondering who that 1 per cent is benefiting. It benefits the mortgage lender, but he already has the mortgage on

the building in these days when the value of mortgages on homes has certainly not gone down. So we find we have well in excess of $300 million sitting in trust with CMHC. Since the consumer pays that 1 per cent, it would be a saving right off the top if the minister could eliminate it. The mortgage lender does not need the extra protection since he has the protection of the mortgage, and certainly there is no mortgage in this country that would not pay itself out.
My final point before the minister answers my questions is to congratulate him upon his appointment. I have been sitting here all day listening to the minister answer questions. I wish we had had the same type of co-operation yesterday from the Minister of Transport.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Madam Chairman, with reference to mortgage insurance, the 1 per cent charge has been a standard charge which, incidentally, applies to private insurers also. It is profitable for the corporation, but there are losses, I was surprised to hear that. This gives them a sense of security, and it also enables the lender to lower preferred rates. There are advantages that way, too. I might have more to say about this in relation to other matters and warranties at a future date-not too far in the future, I hope.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, followed by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham.

Madam Chairman, as the minister is aware, there are several questions that I have been discussing with him. One relates to factory relocation. The minister is aware of the issue in my riding of Surrey-White Rock. I should like to ask him what kind of funding is available under Bill C-27. What kind of budgetary allotment has been made in that bill?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: There are no specific limits on funds. Of course, it has to be approved by the provinces and submitted to the federal government, but generally speaking we will fund a reasonable program. For the study it is 50-50; that is, 50 per cent between the federal government and the province and/or municipalities who have a great stake in it. Some provinces may accept that or may want to share it with the municipalities. It would vary depending on what costs the municipality had that were not directly related. There are no limits on it, depending on the scope of the program, but there is responsibility on both sides.
If we hurry this up we will have the department "danson" well. Maybe not barn dancing, but "danson". On this side of the House we are not very intellectual, so we will have to try harder.
Hear, hear!
Honesty is always the best policy.

How would you know? Madam Chairman, there is another problem and that is the administration of CMHC. First, we are all aware that there are several regulations that are imperative if the low dividend program is to work. One is that there is a limitation on
October 24, 1974

lending; another is that it is supposed to be ascribed to low income families-and each of those words is operative in that term. Officially, there is supposed to be an affidavit of earnings given by the people who will make use of the program.
I recognize that it is difficult to police all the areas that are making use of this program. As a matter of fact, the chairman of CMHC in Vancouver, who is directing his attention to the limited dividend program, said the program is open to abuse by developers and that proper policing would take "an army of inspectors". I suggest this man has adopted the same attrition policy that the Minister of National Defence has been using.
I am concerned because I thought there was an oversight. I investigated on my own and found that the only question being asked was, "Do you have a family?" No question was asked about income. The only restriction was whether or not one had a family. If one had a family, there were no apartments available. And that was supposed to be for low income families. If one did not have a family, they had an apartment available right away, especially on the second and third floors because there were two and three-bedroom apartments there. I asked how this could be, if they were restricting families to the lower floors, and what did people with the two and three-bedroom apartments on the second and third floors do with them, and I was told that they could convert one room into a den. This is housing for low income families in Surrey, where there is a zero vacancy rate. People are waiting for two and three-bedroom apartments, and this sort of thing is going on.
At the time this situation was discovered the former minister said he would initiate an investigation. I recognize that the present minister was not the cause of this problem, but he has responsibility for it now. I should like to ask him whether that investigation has been conducted, and if it has, what was discovered? Then I have some more questions, Madam Chairman.
