speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to discuss the estimates of the Department of National Defence for 1974-75 and to discuss with members of the committee the outstanding service provided by the Canadian armed forces. It might be helpful if I outlined the over-all financial position for the current year now under review. I also want to share with members of the committee my thoughts about the financing of the defence program.
First, may I emphasize that in dollar terms the defence budget has not been cut. It has been increased substantially. The blue book of estimates will show that we were to spend this year, the year under consideration, $2,360 million, or some $144 million more than last year. That $144 million represents approximately the 7 per cent increase which was approved in the financing formula we started on last year.
In addition-this is even more significant-we expect before the end of this year to have approval from the government to spend another $140 million on top of that 7 per cent increase. This means that the defence budget for the current year will be more than one quarter of a billion dollars, almost $300 million, greater than last year. It must be evident, therefore, that the defence budget has not been cut.
We in National Defence are aware, as are all other departments and all citizens, that rapidly rising prices are a major problem. We saw, when planning early in the fiscal year, that if we had adopted the over-all program, if we had got everything we wanted, we would have been another $100 million over even an expanded budget, one that was up by more than a quarter of a billion dollars. In order to reduce expenditures and prevent that almost uncontrolled expansion of expenditure, we took the steps I shall describe.
Essentially, we reduced expenses in four areas. First, by natural attrition the strength of the force in numbers went from about 82,000 to about 79,000. Through that attrition process we achieved an expenditure saving of more than $50 million. Second, we made reductions in operations, that is, in areas such as fuel consumption and travel. The reduction in operations for the current year represents a saving of $12 million. Third, we stretched out the procurement process and in that way, while trying to maintain all essential capital requirements, cut expenditures by $23 million. Finally and fourthly, we took a hard look at the purchasing program. As hon. members know, we have a very big inventory. We found that by better inventory management, by not having more then we need on our shelves and by introducing a new system, we were actually able to save this year $13 million.
These figures add up to about $98 million, or approximately the $100 million by which we would have been over even an expanded budget if we had not taken these steps. These reduced expenditures have enabled us to stay within the budget, even though it is up almost $300 million. We have stayed within a budget which is not out of control and which is reasonable for the current year.
The strength of the force has declined, as I said, to 79,000 personnel. With that number we cannot expect to perform the same tasks as we could perform with a larger force. Therefore, it will be necessary for us to balance the tasks and commitments of the armed forces with the smaller numbers available to perform those tasks.
I now want to speak about the important work the Canadian armed forces have been asked to do by the government. I think that when we consider all these tasks and commitments we will realize that little we will discuss in this debate on the estimates is more important to the armed forces and to Canada than the issues involved in the four central tasks of the Canadian armed forces.
The first task, and the one to which we give the highest priority, is nothing less than the defence of our sovereignty, the maintenance of Canadian independence. I have spoken of this in some detail on other occasions and I do not intend to elaborate on it at this point. Everyone will agree that this role is vital.
The second task is to participate with the United States in the defence of North America. In this connection we think of the very important and close relationship we have with the great neighbour who shares this continent with us. This is a most important subject and one which really goes beyond the role of the forces themselves.
The third task of the armed forces is to work with our NATO partners to carry forward the concept of collective

October 24, 1974

security and to participate in the collective defence of the free world. When we conceive of our various relationships with Europe, can we think of another which is closer or more important than the fact that more than 5,000 members of the Canadian armed forces live in western Europe-their families are with them; their children go to school there? That is a link of measureless importance to our relationship with those countries.
The fourth great task is our new and vital role in trying to help achieve international stability, the role called peacekeeping, one in which Canada has demonstrated not only leadership moral but very practical leadership to the world. Those are our four great tasks, and when hon. members stop to think of them they will realize they are among the most important issues which can come before this committee.
I want to point out that when we are thinking about defence policy, when we are thinking of the taxpayers' money being spent on defence, there is very much more than the more apparent benefit to be considered. Indeed, the taxpayer gets double value for money spent on national defence-sometimes more than double value. There are other benefits; perhaps they could be described as hidden benefits, but they are nevertheless very real. I need hardly remind the committee of the great economic benefit which results from the payroll to communities directly affected. We only have to try to close, not a base but a small station somewhere and immediately we begin to hear about the great impact this would have on the economy of the region. We do not hear so much when everything is going along normally, but when we try to close a base we soon find out the benefit which it has brought to the community. But more important than the payroll or even the economic benefit is the benefit to industry which accrues from the expenditure of tax dollars for defence. I refer to the new technology which is being developed and to the jobs which are provided in advanced technology particularly in the electronics industry. This is of great significance to Canada.
There is yet another area, one which is not so well recognized by the public. A significant portion of the tax dollars used for defence are used to meet the cost of training. We in National Defence are the largest vocational training and educational institute in Canada. We have some 90 trades, and today there are literally tens of thousands of men and women in Canada who are doing better for themselves and for their country as a result of the training they received because we spent National Defence dollars on their training. This is a hidden benefit which should be remembered when considering defence expenditures.
I could go on to give a long list of other benefits which are sometimes overlooked, but I shall not go into detail. All hon. members are aware of our youth program, the cadets. They are aware of our work in opening the north, in establishing airports there. They know that we are involved in the protection of the environment, that we have a responsibility not only for identifying oil slicks but for clearing them up when they occur. For these tasks, we have both the expertise and the equipment.
Hon. members are aware of the support we are given- perhaps not as much as some who sit across the way would
Estimates
like-in identifying foreign vessels which have entered our fishing waters. These are all ways in which the defence dollar is spent for the benefit of Canada. Canadian forces are involved in assisting at major sporting events such as the PanAmerican Games and the Olympic Games. Then there are ceremonial events. Some of these go almost unnoticed, but they are wanted by the Canadian people. Search and rescue is another example.
I could go on to list other benefits Canada is receiving when we spend defence dollars. However, what I want to say is that the real question, the simple question facing us today in National Defence is this: how do we continue to perform those four important tasks and provide the other benefits I have described in days when the cost of everything we require is rising rapidly, and still manage to stay within a budget which does not reach uncontrolled limits?
There are some answers which will have to be considered by this committee and by my colleagues in cabinet. One answer is, of course, to provide a great deal more money. But there are limits. Important as it is that we should have more money, there are clearly limits in days when we want to restrain our expenditure. The answer of granting unlimited funds is not possible in today's world. The other thing to do is to balance our tasks with the tax dollars we can obtain.
Whatever amount of money we finally spend in the future, one thing is certain: we will have to change the ratio between our expenditures for personnel, operations and capital. We will have to increase the percentage spent for capital and new equipment and for operations. At the present time, as I believe most hon. members know, we are spending 67 per cent of our budget for pay and allowances, 22 per cent for operations and 11 per cent for new equipment.
If I may conclude very briefly, Madam Chairman, it is against this background that I believe the estimates should be considered this evening. I have simply tried to point out to the committee that the defence budget has not been cut in dollar terms, but substantially increased. The four central tasks of national defence are important to Canada and all of us here are involved. I look for hon. members' help in deciding what to do with these really big issues-big issues, not just for defence but for all of us in Canada. There are other benefits accruing to the taxpayer that must be considered.

Madam Chairman, I should first like to say a word about the last two days in this House and the benefits of the committee of supply. I have been here for about two years and I have heard a great deal of discussion about the committee of supply and what a boon it was to the House in keeping the power of debate and decisionmaking within the House. I had never realized how much cabinet ministers are protected during the question period by the rules and customs applicable to that period. Last night was quite a change for ministers from the usual question period, with the routine of one question, two supplementaries and then a question from a different member to a different minister. I suggest that those who believe parliament to be the supreme authority in the land now realize more than ever just what the Liberals took

October 24, 1974
Estimates
away from parliament by the rule changes in 1968 which they enforced by the use of closure.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the presentation of the Minister of National Defence. Since I was not in the House on October 15, 1974, it was very gracious of the minister to repeat tonight what he said then. I was hoping that he was going to answer the important question that is before all Canadians now, and that is: can the armed forces cope with its current roles and tasks? There is a great divergence of opinion on this subject.
I knew the minister was going to say, before he said it, that he would increase expenditure on capital equipment.
I	do not want to say that the minister has deliberately misled the House or the nation. I did not say that he was doing it deliberately last October when he said that there was a 7 per cent increase in his budget, and that this annual increase would allow for a substantial increase in capital expenditure. I did not say that he was deliberately misleading the House the other day, when he said, "We will use the payroll which would have been used to pay someone not now a member of the armed forces to buy equipment." I do not know whether he was deliberately misleading the House when he said, "What we must aim at is an elite force made up of well equipped and well motivated personnel."
To illustrate my cynicism and the cynicism of the forces themselves to this kind of statement, I should like to go over a few previous statements by Liberal ministers in this regard. I quote from the white paper on defence of 1964:
The total savings to be effected as a result of such reductions will make available funds for capital equipment purchases, and eventually make possible more equitable distribution of the defence dollar between equipment and housekeeping costs.
Does that sound familiar, Madam Chairman? Again, a Liberal Minister of National Defence, on May 8, 1964 said:
This reduction ... will assist us in the difficult task of getting our defence expenditures back in balance. We must increase the proportion of funds available for new equipment if we are to have a viable and effective force in the years to come. The present proportion of about 14 per cent for equipment is unacceptably low and must be increased to something in the order of 25 per cent in the years ahead. Even this proportion is not high compared to other forces.
I think the minister said our present proportion is about
II	per cent, though I think he has "upped" it by about .8 per cent, according to the reference I have. Again, in July of 1964 a Liberal minister promised as follows:
We are going to make whatever savings we can in other areas, in logistics, training and area commands so we will have the maximum savings available for the purchase of new equipment for our armed forces.
Then in February, 1966, this was said by a Liberal cabinet minister:
Program changes had to go through the whole system and the amount of time consumed was so great that the project momentum was often lost and the initial Canadian advantage overtaken by development projects in other countries.
The classic example is the armoured personnel carrier, the Bobcat V.C.
Then he went on to say, believe it or not:
An example of the improved flexibility is in respect to the interesting development of a full scale prototype of an ocean-going hydrofoil vessel.

What an improvement! Then may I quote another authority, who in this House said in 1966:
We have heard statements emanating from the minister's office to the effect... that the savings to be derived from the new policy can be devoted to the acquisition, as the minister likes to put it, of military hardware. On the other hand, having listened to members of the opposition such as the hon. member for Calgary North-
That was the Hon. D. S. Harkness, a former minister.
-it becomes clear that the government has not in fact succeeded in diverting any of these rumoured savings into the acquisition of better and more modern weaponry.
I am of the opinion that the public relations efforts that went into this ... have been very expensive and I am not sure that this has not succeeded in giving the people of this country ... an entirely misleading and false impression of the reality of the situation. It seems that we are looking at a hoax of epic proportions because it does not appear possible that Canada's defence capability has been improved-
That was said by Mr. Ed Schreyer. The following quotation sounds exactly like the one in the statement of the minister tonight. This is what a former Liberal minister said in 1967:
One of the stated intentions of the savings that could be made was to use those savings for new equipment for the armed forces. No one regrets more than I do that last year we were not able to increase the amount of money being spent... I hope that there will be a very substantial improvement in the coming fiscal year-
A question was put on the order paper in October, 1967, by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. He asked:
In view of the information revealed by an answer tabled in this House last Monday, which indicated that Canada's armed forces have suffered a reduction in personnel from 123,000 to 105,000 over the past three years, could the minister indicate whether this process of attrition is to continue indefinitely or whether there is an absolute floor; and if so, what that floor is?
This was the answer by the Hon. Leo Cadieux, the then minister of national defence:
This is a very broad question. I prefer to answer by saying I hope we can have adequate forces to meet our commitments.
Then on March 1, 1968, the same minister said this:
We have fixed the floor at 100,000 and I hope we can stay there. This is what I consider a minimum to meet the commitments that we have.
There has not been one commitment involving more than 300 to 400 men lifted from the armed forces from that day to this. Then, again, he said in June of 1969:
We have concluded that a regular force of 80,000 to 85,000 will be needed to meet Canada's defence requirements ... Basic to our planning was a firm decision to concentrate wherever possible, on reducing administrative and support activities, to provide us with a higher ratio of operational to non-operational forces than in the past.
Then on October 10, 1973, the present minister had this to say:
This annual increase will allow for substantial increases in capital expenditure, particularly for greatly needed new equipment.
After 10 years of Liberal ministers cutting back personnel and buying new equipment the minister last October found himself repeating the same old song, that at the present time National Defence is spending approximately 11 per cent of its budget for new equipment and facilities. He said that under the modernization and renewal program almost 20 per cent of the total budget would be spent for new equipment by the end of the 1970's. He now announces that this plan, which was supposed to last until
October 24, 1974

the end of the 70's, is now as dead as the dodo. The minister stated that the new formula would solve this problem which has plagued the department for so many years, that is, too low a percentage of the defence budget being used for capital equipment.
On October 15 of this year the minister said:
The only way we can improve the military capability and the conditions of the present members of the armed forces is to reduce the number of recruits taken in and put on the payroll. To state the equation in the simplest possible way-we are going to use the payroll that would have been used to pay someone not now a member of the armed forces to buy equipment and improve conditions for the people now in the armed forces.
It is no wonder the minister is unwittingly deceiving the people of Canada. The record is there. This is the same speech made once a year for about 10 years by Liberal ministers of national defence, yet the result has been exactly the same in every year. A person could look through the estimates here and spend hours talking about various items. Let me try to get two or three questions answered by the minister.
The present situation is, in my mind, so serious it has led to hitherto unheard of protests from senior serving officers. General Garton said the other day that we will have to reduce instruction and flying time. Admiral Boyle said that he cannot carry out our roles with fewer men and will need to cancel training exercises.
General Dextraze said in a news letter in September that he knew that rumours have been circulating to the effect that we are about to have our staff reduced again, but these rumours are untrue. It does not seem to me that the Chief of the Defence Staff would put his signature to such a statement to counter the rumour if he had not previously consulted with the Minister of National Defence. Will the minister tell us what consultation took place in September before the Chief of Defence Staff wrote that letter denying any cutback in personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I should first of all like to say to the hon. member for Victoria that in his recounting of the history of statements of past ministers of defence he has not really been stating the facts as they appear in the blue books. I would draw his attention to what we are studying, that is, pages 15-6 and 15-7 of the estimates, where he will see that the expenditures for capital equipment increased from $172 million in the year 1972-73, to $228 million in the year 1973-74, and up to $270 million for 1974-75, after the economies mentioned previously. This constitutes an increase of more than $100 million in that two year period.
What did you buy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We could give you the full list. We have been moving in the direction I have stated; in my judgment perhaps not moving as rapidly as we would like, but certainly moving in that direction.
I was looking at these figures when the hon. member referred to a statement by the chief of staff. I would appreciate it if the hon. member would ask the question again if he wishes me to comment on it.

Madam Chairman, I hesitate to ask the question again because the minister has used up three or four of my allotted minutes not answering my question. I was curious to know whether there was any consultation
Estimates
between the Minister of National Defence and the Chief of the Defence Staff before he issued the statement in September denying the rumour that the forces were to be cut down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I assume that the hon. member is referring to the personal message the chief of staff wrote to the armed forces. He writes in a very personal way, and naturally what he says reflects conversations he has had with me. As I have said here in this House and in committee, I am in complete agreement with the chief of staff on the fact that if the number of personnel is to be reduced the tasks must be reduced, and that is what the chief of staff said in that letter.

I take it there was consultation between the minister and the Chief of Defence Staff, and the minister agreed to the sending out of that message which gave the impression that the forces were not to be cut, yet the minister is telling us that there are defence cuts, and that the force is to be reduced by the process of attrition. The minister has put the Chief of the Defence Staff in an absolutely impossible situation. I do not know whether the minister believed, at the time he was consulting with the Chief of Defence Staff, that there were to be no cuts in personnel, but if he did he must then have been misled by somebody else, possibly the cabinet. I should like to have more detail on this if the minister can give it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are two points involved here. First, at the time of that letter in September, the strength of the armed forces was at 79,000 and, secondly, that type of letter is not one in respect of which the chief of staff would consult with me regarding every sentence and paragraph. I will say, however, that he certainly has reflected the policy of the department as I have outlined it.

Then I can only assume that the betrayal goes one level higher, and that the minister has been suffering under the delusion that he was going to get funds which the cabinet is not now willing to give. My time is just about up, and I would hate to sit down without trying to be a little more constructive about defence than one could possibly be in this milieu.
I have been getting more concerned each year about the way the money is going out from the minister's office and department, and particularly the small amount being apportioned to the purchase of equipment. What is really needed is for the minister to decide on a plan which is not based on dollars, because under this Liberal administration the dollar is the least reliable measure of any, with the value of the dollar going down each year. Anyone who suggests that last year the 7 per cent increase in the budget would look after things simply does not know the facts of life.
The minister must come up with a plan based on how big a force he wants, how he wants it armed and equipped, and then if it is based on five years he should say to his masters: "If you do not agree to this, fire me. If you do agree, don't welsh on it later".

Madam Speaker, there is in our view nothing sacrosanct about military spending as such. It is often

Defence who told us in plain words that this form of defence is no longer practical. I should like the minister to grasp the nettle now and, instead of being slightly evasive, frankly say that this form of defence is not good and we will not proceed with it. He should say that there will be some expenditures for the defence of our sovereignty, and he should mention what he believes is necessary so that we can examine that on its own merit, without pretending that it has something to do with NORAD.
So far as NORAD is concerned I think there would be a sigh of relief by the Canadian people if we showed the gumption to get out of something that has made no sense at any time, or at least not for the past ten years or so.
There is one other matter I should like to raise. I know others wish to speak and I shall therefore be brief. This subject was raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt, in a question a day or so ago. I want to ask the minister about a certain report. I have it from a magazine called Latin America of October 18, 1974, to the effect that a Canadian mission from the Department of Supply and Services and the Department of National Defence, headed by Colonel Basil Collett went, to Brazil in order to look over the purchase of an armoured car which would replace what I understand to be completely worn out armoured cars that we have now. I would like to know whether they want to do that and whether the figures are in the neighbourhood of $200 million or $300 million.
I should like to ask the minister whether he has consulted the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the impact of such a purchase. Is he aware that Brazil is governed by a military dictatorship, and that many other countries in South America would view such purchases with very grave apprehension? We cannot do these things in one department without taking account of what should be happening in another. I think that Canadians are aware of this because this magazine tells me that Colonel Collett was instructed to maintain a non military profile during his tour of Brazil. I do not know whether or not that is so, but there will be strong political opposition at home and among our NATO allied, as well as in South America, to this sort of purchase.
I hope that the minister will be able to tell us that that will not be the source. How are we going to pay for them? Will we pay bolstering up the present regime in Brazil with other military supplies? That is what Brazil's neighbours in South America feel. I ask the minister to tell us whether these facts are reasonably outlined. I can give him the name of the company with which we are supposed to be dealing, and I could give him more details if he is interested in seeing them. But I would like to hear how far we have proceeded toward this particular purchase, and I want to suggeest to him that it has political implications that should be examined before any such purchase is concluded.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, let me say in answer to the last question raised that this is just a matter of what we call sourcing, or finding the areas where we might be able to acquire the kind of equipment that we need, and to make comparisons with what is available in other countries. The negotiations in this respect are not
Estimates
far advanced, and are not at a stage at which it would be necessary for me to consult the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Now, if I may, I should like to comment briefly on the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood because he has expressed his views to me very clearly a number of times on NORAD. I would like to suggest to him that we are not in as fixed a situation as he implies- we do make changes from time to time. We have closed down three radar stations this year that were part of the NORAD set up. We have reduced the number of our CF 100's to nine. We are certainly following closely the changes that the Americans are making in their reduction of interceptor aircraft. We are quite capable of making adjustments in NORAD. As I have said before, we do not have to make changes in the agreement because, as the hon. member knows, the NORAD agreement does not specify any equipment. I can assure him that we have an open mind, and we pay very careful attention to his views.

Madam Chairman, it is hardly worth while for me even to take a deep breath because it is almost six o'clock. I have some remarks that I would like to make through you to the minister and, after I make them I should like to put some questions to him as well. I think that at this time I will spin it out until six o'clock, if I may, because I do not think it is worth starting now and then trying to break off my remarks.
Generally speaking, I sympathize very much with the problem the minister has with his budget. I support a strong military force in this country, a well equipped and well trained military force, and I am in favour of seeing them have the best possible equipment. I hope that we will be able to maintain a force in the order of 90,000 to 100,000-not the much scaled down force we have now.
I am afraid that if this scaling down continues, as my colleague has illustrated for us, we will arrive at a point in time, five, six or ten years from today, when we will be looking at a force of perhaps 35,000 or 40,000. I recognize that there are people in this country who would like to see our armed forces reduced to nothing more than a national police force, but I am not one who supports that idea. So I can tell the minister that if he is in favour of improving the position of our armed forces, of equipping them adequately to do a proper job and of maintaining a good strong presence, then I will support him.
May I call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. When the House rose at six o'clock, the committee was considering Bill C-31, more specifically the votes for the Department of National Defence which appear on page 16 of the bill.

October 24, 1974
Estimates

Mr. Chairman, I had just started my remarks about five minutes to six so I have some time left. I was saying to the minister, through you, that I am a very great supporter of the armed forces and I hope the plan for the future would be to increase their number rather than reduce it. I would like to see the level at 90,000 or 100,000, rather than see it cut to about 70,000 as is the suggestion now. If we keep changing ministers of national defence as we have done in the last few years, I suppose in a few years time we will see a different minister here telling us that we can get along with 50,000 but that they will be better fed, better clothed, better paid and they will still do the job we want.
I am very disturbed at the prospect of a cut in the armed forces, and I do not accept that we have actually increased the dollar amount of the defence budget. The fact is that its share of the GNP has gone down considerably between 1968 and 1974. In the 1968-69 budget it was allocated 16.4 per cent, and today it gets 11 per cent of the federal budget. Inflation is eating away our armed forces, and their equipment in particular in a very disastrous way.
In the last four or five years we have had four ministers of national defence and, as one of my colleagues mentioned already, each has come to us with the same story. I get pretty upset about the attitude toward the portfolio of national defence and its position in the cabinet. I am not one who likes to take personal shots at individuals but I feel that the national defence portfolio is a sort of catchall-a place where they drop people when they do not know where else to put them. This is the inference we have to draw in light of so many changes over the years.
Surely if there is a good minister in the portfolio they should leave him there and let him carry their plans through. We will have one minister who will expound a theory or lay down some procedure, and then another one will come along and say it cannot be done. This appears to be a sort of game, but a dangerous one.
If we should continue with the present defence policy I am afraid that in an emergency, national or international, we could not respond adequately. When I see that we have destroyers but no crews, that we have tanks that we cannibalize to keep other tanks going, that we have aircraft that we cannibalize for other aircraft, and obsolete motor vehicles procured in 1952, I must conclude that we are in pretty bad shape. My colleague says some of the motor vehicles could be sold as antiques, and perhaps if we keep them for another 20 years they could. The danger is that the longer we delay procurement the more it is going to cost. I am sure the minister realizes this.
When the minister says that we are going to cut this capital expenditure and that capital expenditure and thus will be able to cut $100 million or so out of our estimates, he is really saying that these aircraft, trucks, tanks and naval vessels that we are going to procure some time in the future will cost maybe 50 per cent more than they would today.
The other matter that concerns me is our northern sovereignty. I have read a great deal about this, and a lot of passionate words have been spoken on the subject. I have read the views of the United States. I wonder what is happening when I see that they have commissioned two of
[The Chairman.)
the largest icebreakers in the world, larger than anything afloat today even in Russia or Finland. These are certainly not going to be used in the Caribbean; they are going to be used in the Arctic. Do we have the capability of defending our northern sovereignty? I do not think so. I do not think we have either the equipment or the personnel to do very much about it.
I have about five minutes left, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to ask the minister a few short questions and I would appreciate short answers.
First, what have we done regarding the replacement of motor vehicles? Are we going to let contracts, have they been let, and for how many vehicles?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have started to replace our vehicles, having purchased about 500 new trucks. We need many more. We are negotiating for the purchase of more than 2,000 114 ton trucks. Our truck procurement program is just starting and is not far advanced.
May I comment about the hon. member's statement. He said that the portfolio of national defence was a catch-all. I think those were his words. May I reply?
I meant nothing personal.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I realize that. Because many dedicated men and women serve in the armed forces, and because I am responsible for spending more than 10 per cent of the federal budget my portfolio is-and I am not saying this because I am the minister-one of the most important portfolios in the government. On behalf of the armed forces that should be recorded.

I accept that. I did not mean anything personal. I made the observation because one minister comes in, lasts about 18 months, and is replaced by another, and so on. This, I think, is a downgrading of the armed forces. I made my comment in all sincerity, without wishing to make a personal comment about the minister himself.
I am concerned about the procurement program for the 114 ton vehicles, but I am also concerned about tracked vehicles. How are negotiations for these 1 !4 ton vehicles proceeding? How close are we to procurement? Where do we stand with regard to the tracked over-the-snow vehicle so desperately required in the north?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we have conducted negociations in both of these areas for many months, and those involving tracked and over-the-snow vehicles are close to completion. As soon as we resolve some money questions which, as you know, are under discussion, we hope to go ahead with both programs.
Will the government procure these in 1975 or 1976? When will we have some of these vehicles in our possession?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I hope to have them early in 1975. That is my intention.
October 24, 1974

Mr. Chairman, does the Department of National Defence intend to expand the role of our armed forces in northern Canada? I am particularly concerned about the north in view of the remarks the minister made about the environment, roadbuilding, and our position in northern Canada. I assume that the plan to procure tracked vehicles is part of an over-all plan to increase our presence in northern Canada. Would the minister comment on that?
The minister spoke about cutting $100 million from our defence budget. Last week, according to Newsweek magazine, we lent $100 million to Iran. That country, in turn, bought from the United States tremendous quantities of military hardware. It spent almost twice as much as we spent on our national defence budget. The people of Canada would have been served better if we had not lent Iran $100 million at 7 per cent but kept the money for our defence budget. That was only a comment. Would the minister care to speak on the northern aspect I mentioned earlier?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I said in the statement I made at the beginning of our examination of my estimates, one of the important roles for the Canadian armed forces is that of participating in the opening of the Canadian north. We are proceeding with what we call the new Viking program, under which 125 men go north, live, and work under northern conditions, and test equipment. Within the last year we opened the Arctic training centre at Churchill, Manitoba, and our forces will train there regularly from now onwards. May I mention that ships of the fleet sailed into Hudson Bay this summer for the first time on training exercises, demonstrating that Canada is not bounded by two oceans but by the three oceans. We are doing a number of things, as I have mentioned, to make our presence felt in the north, and this, I believe, will increase rather than diminish as we proceed.
Mr. Chairman, it is a great pleasure to address this august assembly for the first time.
Hear, hear!

Defence policy has been much criticized in the past. People say that we spend too much, that we have not spent enough, that our forces are underequipped or they are overequipped, that we should increase our commitment to NORAD, and that we should get out of NORAD.
The minister said that in these inflationary times he will try to keep his budget within reason, because the government is committed to showing restraint in its dealings; otherwise, how can it expect the Canadian people to follow its example if it throws money away as if money were going out of style?
Let me reminisce about defence policy during the time when the Liberals were not in power. It interests me, because I was in the Royal Canadian Air Force at the time.
Hear, hear!

During the period 1956-1962 we needed a new long-range patrol aircraft. Air Defence Command
Estimates
needed a new high performance aircraft. That new aircraft was on the drawing board. It was known as the Arrow.
Oh, oh!

That piece of new equipment was killed deader than a dormouse by those who now sit across the floor from me. There was a need for new equipment then also.
The matter of personnel, discussed in great detail recently, also concerned us then. In 1962 three permanent commissions were granted in Air Defence Command- Mr.Chairman, that was three in all Canada! You may think morale is low now. Let me say that morale today is pretty good when compared with what it was during that period.
During that period people who had been trained as air crew were put on flying duties for a three year term and then transferred automatically to ground duties-this after many thousands of dollars had been spent on their training. That practice has now been changed.
Then again, during the last real crisis we experienced, the Cuban missile crisis, the airforce was using an aircraft the C101, which had been accepted from the United States to replace the Arrow. It was an aircraft in no way comparable to the Arrow. However, at that time we did not possess a single effective weapon in Canada. If bombers came over Canada there was no way of striking at them since National Defence policy had failed to provide us with the necessary weapons.
There has been talk regarding NORAD. Certain hon. members feel we should leave this organization and that Canada should not defend its territory. I say we have a duty to take part in the defence of Canadian sovereignty, regardless of the cost of that commitment. The theory appears to be that there is no menace from Russian aircraft at the present time. I would be happy to believe this if I saw evidence that the Russians were dismantling their bombing fleet, but since this is not the case, and since their bombers are carrying atomic weapons, I think there must be a threat from that direction.
It was not missiles which delivered the bombs in Korea or in Viet Nam; it was conventional bombers. For this reasons I shall support NORAD until I see that the other side is reducing its own force. It seems odd that we should have to stand here and defend our position. Why should we have to feel guilty about protecting our country? We think it is right, and that we have a duty to maintain these defences.
There has been some debate regarding our membership in NATO. I think that over the years NATO has been the deterrent which has kept Europe free.
Tell the Prime Minister!

As long as I have some say in it we shall continue our present posture toward NATO.
With regard to our commitments as a peacekeeping force, I believe the world recognizes the contribution Canada has made. We are ih a special position as a nation

October 24, 1974
Estimates
whose forces can operate on the soil of other nations because we do not seek to increase our territory; we are not a warring nation. The respect which we enjoy among other countries in the world bodes well for Canada.
The primary objective of our defence policy must be the maintenance of Canadian sovereignty. There is no disagreement about that. As a nation of 22 million people we cannot compete with the United States or with the U.S.S.R. in defence research and multi-billion dollar defence projects. Modern armaments are expensive, and by the time new projects leave the drawing board they are obsolete. At the present time our defence posture requires new ships, new planes and other new military equipment, but we cannot get all these things at once, especially during a period of inflation when we must all show restraint. I support the position taken by the minister when he says we are trying to live within our budget and restrain our spending.
Would the hon. member answer a question?
By all means.
May I congratulate the hon. member who has just spoken, if this was his first speech in this chamber, as I understand it to have been. It was delivered with great capability. My question is this-

Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to raise a point of order in the middle of a question by the hon. member for Greenwood. I do so because I was informed by the Chair that, having exhausted 20 minutes of my first opportunity to speak, I would not be allowed to take part in the debate again. I have no objection to the hon. member for Greenwood being allowed to ask a question, provided I am given a similar courtesy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Comox-Alberni took only about eight minutes of his time, after which he allowed a question. A question is normally allowed by the Chair in those circumstances.

I do not know if the hon. member was in the chamber when the question of NORAD was discussed this afternoon. I referred to a statement made by the Secretary of Defence Schlesinger which referred to the air defence conducted through NORAD-he did not actually use the word "NORAD"-and in that statement he said: "Because there is no defence against missiles, defence against manned bombers is not practicable". If the hon. member is not prepared to accept my advice-and I would not blame him for that-is he not prepared to give some weight to the words of the Secretary of Defence in the United States?

I am aware of that statement, but I am also aware of the fact that the United States has not dismantled its NORAD equipment. So I can only assume that the capability is still there. Then again, Mr. Schlesinger is but a person; I should like to have the opportunity

to question him about the point of view he has expressed. I should like to know the context in which he made that statement. What does the defence staff think of it? What do the joint chiefs of staff think about that opinion? At any rate they have not put it into practice. Until such time as that friendly nation, which is still carrying a tremendous stock of manned bombers, takes action to cut its fleet I think it is mandatory that we give our support to NORAD.

Would the hon. member accept one more question? In the course of his speech he said that some people were complaining about the forces being over-equipped. Could he identify the people who made that particular claim?

The hon. member is quite correct. We have all recently emerged from an election campaign. This matter was raised in my area-some people were saying there is too much of this and too much of that. It is inevitable that people will take sides. I was referring, really, to the money we were spending. This particular point was not made here in this chamber but during the election campaign.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate, and I should like to tell the minister that I intend to express a few frank views about the situation in defence as I see it. Anything that I say is to the minister in his capacity as minister and in no way reflects on any personal friendship I had with the minister before my remarks, and I hope will have when I have finished my remarks.
In light of some of the things occurring today as well as some of the matters the minister has under study, I would say the situation is so serious that, even though I should like to ask a multiplicity of questions, as others have, this is not time to talk tamely but to talk frankly.
I was disappointed in the extreme that the minister, in presenting his estimates to this committee, gave an apologia, as he did also last time he presented his estimates, as well as in the statement he gave the committee a week or two ago. He sounded more like a stockbroker flipping coupons and juggling figures than a minister expressing the concern of all of those who have a sincere interest in the defence of this country.
He justified a saving of $100 million, and yet when we look at the LIP program some $90 million has been spent. No one suggests that the budget has been cut, but some budgets have been cut by the government in the last few years. The minister could have said some substantive things about defence when he dealt with the four priority tasks of our forces, but he got involved in this semantic debate about figures, taking $17 million here and $14 million there, and ending up with $100 million. If he wants to be Auditor General I think he should move on to other pastures and not confuse serious issues.
The issues are serious because we have had a defence freeze for four years. We have also had a galloping rate of inflation of 15 per cent in terms of service procurement, not 7 per cent which was the yardstick in the formula introduced last year. It is a futile exercise to talk about a
October 24, 1974

cut in the budget, because we know that due to inflation and the freeze the budget has been effectively cut. More important, the effectiveness of the forces has been substantially reduced.
In all kindness, Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister that the vacillation, not only of himself but of his four predecessors in the last five years, the indecision in leadership still evident in his department, and the retreats from decisions that have been made, have all compounded the problem, so that members of the forces of this land, be they private, corporal or general, are in a state of despair, bewilderment and downright depression, as has seldom been the case in peacetime history.
I say peacetime advisedly, because what a peace it is! For example, look at Cyprus. The minister knows more about Cyprus than I because he has been there. Then there is the Middle East. Those are two hot spots in the world that are tinder dry. Yet the Warsaw pact commitment is getting bigger and bigger every year, at a time when our stature as a component part of NATO is shrinking, as indeed is NATO itself. So one cannot describe conditions today ideally as peacetime conditions.
I am sure Confucius or Joseph Howe would have said that if a country cannot patrol or protect its own borders it will not survive as a state. As far as Canada is concerned, I think the capacity of the forces to patrol our borders, and protect the sovereignty of which we are all so proud, is somewhat limited.
Developing a Canadian identity through cultural programs using the broadcasting media are all to the good. Yet when it comes to being bosses of our own territory, a fundamental function of a sovereign state, I suggest we are missing out. By sovereignty, I mean sovereignty over our own borders and the three seas that surround us.
It is a strange paradox, and a sad commentary, that the cutbacks which the minister talked about, but which he did not define in terms of the four functions, are being made at a time when there is increased emphasis on sovereignty, be it in the Arctic, off our shores, both in connection with the fisheries and the 200 mile limit, or our responsibility to NATO to patrol certain sections of the North Atlantic.
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth would be the last person to show any disrespect for the services, and quite frankly, I thought the minister was indulging in a little political partisanship by casting some reflection on the hon. member. He would be the first to admit, as I think the minister would also, that the peacetime serviceman, even in this sort of pseudo-peace we are in today, is the most maligned and misrepresented individual in the public service. The fact that there have been five ministers since 1968 in this important department, which the minister took pride in today, does not give members of the forces much opportunity to find out who their current minister is, so how can he defend the interests of servicemen and officers?
It is time that the Minister of National Defence did start to defend the forces and to fight for the forces, rather than being an apologist for a government that has no interest in the forces, does not care about the forces, and thinks in the abstract terms of the Prime Minister that some are bad,
Estimates
others are worse, so let us not get involved at all. This is not the kind of leadership that we deserve from a minister of national defence. The minister must become the advocate of the forces.
The minister should tell Canadians the way it is. There are problems in defence, and they should not all rest on the shoulders of the minister. Let him tell Canadians about our contribution to NATO. In the statement that the minister filed before the committee in 1973, he told Canadians that we are thirteenth out of fourteen nations in terms of gross national product contribution. The only country below Canada was, as most members know, Luxembourg, and it can hardly be counted because it has only one battalion which serves in Belgium. So we are really last. Is that the kind of commitment of which the Prime Minister is proud? How can he say, as he said in Brussels today, that Canada is proud to continue playing an important part in NATO, when our percentage support is the lowest on the totem pole? Let the minister tell Canadians that.
Let him also tell Canadians about our responsibilities in the north, about how our air patrols and numbers of men have been substantially cut back, and how the option is open to him to cut them back even further. Let me tell the minister that if one of the options that he is considering becomes reality, then I will do my darndest to make sure that either I leave the House or the minister does. Certainly one of us should go if the minister is serious about one of his options respecting the north.
There must be a presence if you want to have sovereignty. If the minister thinks you can cut back overflights for six months at a time without our presence in the area suffering, then he is more naive than I thought.
Let the minister tell Canadians about NATO. I am not talking just about forces in the north, because that is only one facet of defence. Tell Canadians that this night, and every night for the last month, our aircraft have not been flying as far out into the Atlantic, or as often as they used to do. In fact they are staying pretty close to home. The minister knows that cutbacks have affected Maritime command flights. He should start levelling with Canadians.
Someone recently talked about banana republics. I am sure I could compare the military budgets for 1972-73 of most of the banana republics of South America and would find that they spend more proportionately of their national production on defence than we do here. Tell Canadians what we are doing in respect of NATO. Why is this all shrouded in mystery and secrecy?
If Canadians are not prepared to pay the price of defence then the minister will have the understanding of this House. He cannot have things both ways. The minister cannot make statement after statement, as referred to by the hon. member for Victoria today, in the face of shifts, changes, retreats and reversals in our defence policy-and this has been going on since 1958,-with complete despondency and depression in the service.
The minister said that defence of North America is one of our priorities. One of the reasons we are not sharing and joining in exercises in the north with our American cous-

ins is because of cuts in finances. We can spend $2.5 billion on unemployment insurance and $750 million for consultants' reports, but now we have the minister taking the time of the House telling us what a grand fellow he is because he saved $100 million in the estimates today.
In all seriousness, some poeple in the forces are thinking today that this minister is a fraud if he pretends that we are fulfilling the minister's own four stated objectives.
You don't know what you are talking about.

I am not sure who said that but he should stand up. The minister may not have time to answer my questions as I will likely take up my entire 20 minutes, but let me repeat that the minister is a fraud if he stands in this House tonight and suggests we are presently discharging the four commitments to which he referred-and that was true even before any cutbacks.
There has been some reference to cutbacks to the extent of 30 per cent. Having relation to the four stated objectives, I should like to know where those cutbacks will take place. Surely this is the time for the minister to indicate what are the problems and what he considers should be done. He should let us know if we are going to get out of NATO, cut back on our sovereignty expenditures in the north, cut back on our peacekeeping role, or cut back on our Norad commitments. These are the things we should be hearing about here today rather than references to a savings of $100 million in the over-all defence spending.
What about Cyprus and the Middle East?

I suggest that the President of the Treasury Board knows more about Indians than he does about defence. In any event I have the floor at this time. I do not know how much he knows about Indians, but I think they have scalped him a couple of times.
Shame!
An hon. member shouts "shame". It may have been the hon. member for Vaudreville. He is ashamed everytime he speaks. The minister talks glibly about cutting back 30 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. On a number of occasions I have had to correct members of the opposition. I did not at this time interject, but in any event the county is the county of Vaudreuil.
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to chase after muskrat tracks, I am going after something a little bigger.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard some reference to the fact that this government does not care about the armed forces, and this affects me because I am in this government. I would have hon. members understand that there are many of us who have served, who care about the forces, and who will not accept that kind of criticism.
You have a lot to learn.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Take it to your caucus.
You are not a member of the government and the way you are carrying on you never will be, Buster.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I would suggest to the hon. member that what he is raising is an argument and not a question which relates to his own privilege or the privileges of this House.

Mr. Chairman, I do not have time to indulge in these frivolities and indiscretions of hon. members opposite. If they do not know the difference between the cabinet and a member of parliament they have a great deal to learn about political science. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain is a very delightful gentleman, and I know that after he sits and listen to the contributions of various members he will realize that I am directing my remarks to the government and not to Liberal backbenchers, NDP backbenchers or Conservative backbenchers.
With all due respect his own Prime Minister called members of parliament nobodies.
And he isn't even a somebody.

In any event I will ignore these interventions tonight because I am not going to run through the swamp after muskrat tracks when I can go after the Minister of National Defence.
The minister and his officials talk about cutting back to the extent of 30 per cent. I should like to know how you cut back 30 per cent in respect of a foot soldier. Is he supposed to walk only one mile instead of three?
You cut off part of a leg.

That is about as naive as some of the things the department has done. Obviously when you have moving parts, as you do in the mobile or Maritime commands, you have extra costs for aviation fuel and the like. The minister says we are going to have a well fed, well equipped and well motivated Praetorian Guard. Incidentally, my latin is as good as my French, and my French is not too good.
Let me become serious, Mr. Chairman, as I know I am reaching the end of my time. How can you have such a guard when the forces have no purpose? They cannot have a purpose if the minister makes no commitment.
How can any member of the service, especially one in Maritime Command, believe that this minister has a commitment to the force when the largest single problem the minister has is in terms of the capital cost necessary to replace the LRPA? I will not get into that, but the command most affected by that replacement has never even seen the minister. Its members have never seen even his shadow. Since the hon. member became a minister of the Crown he has not taken it upon himself to get out of Ottawa to make an official visit to Maritime Command. Certainly that alone has not done much for Maritime Command.
Let me conclude by saying that we heard a great deal during the election campaign about leadership. The government received a mandate to lead. It is time the minister started to lead by making some decisions about the forces.
October 24, 1974

Perhaps before he makes those decisions it would be a good idea, both for the minister and the forces, if he moved around the country speaking to service clubs, explaining the problems and the limitations.
Perhaps I could refer to the Minister of Agriculture as an example. I have disagreed with him on many occasions and on many issue, but I respect his energy. He deserves some kudos for his commitments to farmers. I think it is time the Minister of National Defence took a leaf from that minister's book. He should become the spokesman for the armed services just as the egg monster has become the self-styled spokesman for the farmers. Perhaps then he would become known to the servicemen as the Minister of Defence, no longer dominated by his cabinet colleagues or restricted in his activities. Let him start now by meeting his men in the different commands. The minister has been all around the world, but he has not visited his own men in Maritime Command.
I do not know about Mobile Command or Air Transport Command, but Maritime Command, as the minister knows, is one of the biggest problems. It is obvious, because of its moving parts which are involved in the sea or air aspect, that that command is most concerned about the cutbacks in operations. I had intended to read a beautiful speech by Churchill given in 1938 about the annexation of Czechoslovakia but I am afraid that my time is just about up, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

All right. Then by popular request I shall read these words of Mr. Churchill spoken in th House of Commons in England on October 5, 1938. He was the first person who said that Neville Chamberlain came back with an unmitigated defeat. I want to read this seriously because of the problems the minister has and the narrow focus he has on these problems. We are getting close to the same situation.
In talking about Czechoslovakia Mr. Churchill said:
But we cannot consider the abandonment and ruin of Czechoslovakia in the light only of what happened only last month.
I stress that because it is not just a decision about the Argus that is involved; it is the over-all thing.
It is the most grievous consequence which we have yet experienced of what we have done and of what we have left undone in the last five years-five years of futile good intention, five years of eager search for the line of least resistance, five years of uninterrupted retreat of British power, five years of neglect of our air defences. Those are the features which I stand here to declare and which marked an improvident stewardship for which Great Britain and France have dearly to
pay-
That was in 1938. All I can say in closing, especially to my friends to the left, is that men have not died peacefully in their beds since civilization dawned. There has always been some type of war. Mr. Chairman, I want to say that we can get out of that situation, but we are not out of it and we will not get out of it by not protecting ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some of the remarks of the hon. member for Annapolis Valley do not require comment. However, it always comes as a surprise to me, and as a surprise for those of us who are working in the
Estimates
interests of the Canadian armed forces, to find that it is usually the members of the opposition who refer to the Canadian armed forces in the kind of language that I wrote down and which was used by the hon. member- downhearted, ill-equipped and with low morale. I do not know why they seem to want to degrade the Canadian armed forces in that way.
Visit them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do visit the armed forces. I talk frequently with members of the forces and I do not find them downhearted. I find them dedicated. I find them highly professional, efficient and proud of the work they are doing for Canada. I think that if the hon. member for Annapolis Valley had been in the House earlier today he would have heard the importance which I attach to the roles played by the armed forces. I do not intend to repeat my statement now. However, may I say with your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, that if everything was as bad as the hon. member and other hon. members suggest in the past ten years-
I said since 1968.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to read not from an old paper but from something which appeared in an Ottawa paper this afternoon. This may be an indication of whether things are as bad as they are made out to be.
Who wrote it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The name is Robert P. Rothschild. He says:
There is no question but that the Canadian armed forces are about the best-trained and most professional military organizations in the world.
He is a general. He was one of your boys who is now retired. We used to call him the baron, Baron Rothschild.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The last sentence I wish to read states: Their record of achievement has few, if any, equals. The Canadian people have every right to be, and should be, extremely proud of them.
On a point of order-
Oh! Oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I believe the hon. member for Annapolis Valley wishes to raise a point of order, if hon. members will allow me to hear it.

Mr. Chairman, I must say I have been here ever since the debate started. I listened to the minister. So far as General Rothschild, who just retired from defence headquarters, is concerned, the reference to him accentuates my point. How many sergeants messes and corporals messes has the minister visited, and did he get out in the field?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Vancouver South.

Mr. Chairman, through you I should like to put some questions to the minister. The first question

October 24, 1974
Estimates
relates to the air-sea rescue squadron on the west coast, Squadron 442. A year ago I had occasion to ask the minister questions related to the difficulties that squadron was having in maintaining its equipment and keeping all its aircraft in the air for an optimum period of time. The questions I asked and the subsequent debate which took place made it clear-and I know there is no disagreement on this point-that there was no criticism of the squadron and that in fact the men operated as efficiently as possible.
As recorded at page 7213 of Hansard for October 25,1973, I asked the minister the following question:
Will the minister either replace these worn-out aircraft or increase the number available, and when will this be done?
The minister answered in part:
In the new modernization and renewal program that I have announced there are funds for new equipment which will be going into search and rescue, as well as into other areas.
Would the minister tell us exactly what has been done with regard to 442 Squadron further to the comment he made a year ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, broadly speaking the equipment for search and rescue has been maintained and improved. I cannot bring forward the details at this moment to tell you exactly what equipment has been added to 442 Squadron.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if he has any knowledge whether there has been any change in the basic equipment of Squadron 442 in the past year, or whether there has been any change in the procedure of supplying that squadron with replacement parts on a more efficient basis than was the case a year ago?
The minister understands that at the time the problem was to try to take spare parts from a base somewhere in central Canada to British Columbia, and there was a further difficulty in that civil aircraft flying into Comox did not have the capacity to carry many of the parts. Can the minister tell us whether he has any knowledge of any change in the basic equipment, or in the parts replacement system that was in effect at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can understand the hon. member for Vancouver South being interested and concerned about the question of spare parts for the squadron in his region, and I will undertake to provide that information in detail. As I have said earlier, however, I cannot do it at this time.

I thank the minister for his answer. I want to state unequivocally-because there are some members on the government side of the House who seem to think that any criticism coming from this side indicates lack of interest or respect for the armed forces of this country- that, as the minister may know, I served modestly in the armed forces of my country some years ago and I am extremely proud of it. Any comments I have to make are made because I think the armed forces in the country fulfill a very necessary function, and that we are served by dedicated men.

However, I am concerned when I find that cuts are taking place. Also, when I talk to people in the armed forces and we hear unfortunate descriptions of the situation, I find that that can only lead to low morale if it remains uncorrected. I may say to some hon. members who have spoken tonight that I served with the Canadian brigade in Germany in 1953, at which time the government said it was the finest and best equipped brigade that had ever left Canada.
This does not concern the minister, but that sort of statement was made at the time when we served in the infantry brigade in Germany, when we had no web belts and no steel helmets, we were short of munitions, and in fact could not have fought our way out of a wet paper bag because of a basic breakdown in supply and communications. Yet I remember, as a young soldier, the government telling me that it was a marvellous brigade. But I was there and saw things that the then minister of national defence, when he came to visit, never saw because he had no chance to look at men in the line, or to talk to the people who could have told him what was the trouble. So I urge the minister to be sure in all his travels to talk to everyone in the forces, and not just to those who may feel they have to be apologists for him.
I ask the minister to let us know exactly how many front line battalions are stationed presently in Canada. I believe there are nine infantry battalions, and I take it the minister agrees.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the correct number.
Can the minister tell me what is the strength of those battalions? If he cannot tell me the exact number of men, can he give me the approximate strength?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: A battalion is in the order of 600 to 700 men.

Unless battalion strength has been changed drastically since I was in the forces, at which time a battalion at full strength was substantially more than that, is the minister saying that battalions are now running at around 500 or 600 men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I said 600 to 700 men.
Is that the answer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the figure that I have used and understand to be substantially the right figure for the strength of our battalions at present.

May I then ask the minister whether, from a military point of view, looking at what is a full strength battalion on the Canadian battle order, whether these battalions are under strength or up to strength?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Compared with their wartime or fully authorized strength, they are undermanned.

That is the point I am trying to make. I understand that in NATO we have 2,800 ground troops. I should like the minister to tell me how many of that number are actually front line combat troops. I am not talking about medical personnel or other support troops.
