In other words, have we one full strength battalion that could go into action in Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I understand that the correct figure for the land troops in Europe is 3,000.
Of the 3,000, how many are front line combat troops?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: All of the 3,000 are front line troops.
Where else do we have front line combat troops-how many in Cyprus and how many in the Middle East?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In Cyprus we have front line troops numbering 950. Our forces in the Middle East are involved in logistics and are not considered front line in the same sense.

Doing some very rough arithmetic it seems to me that Canada is in a situation of having total front line combat troops numbering less than 11,000 or 12,000 men. I understand that this is less than a division. What I am asking the minister-and I am not asking this in a pejorative sense but in the hope that some support from this side may make it easier for the government in terms of public opinion and in terms of the government's own deliberations-is whether he is satisfied that on a budget of $2.5 million the best Canada can do is to put less than
10,000	men into the front line as combat troops? Is that good enough on that budget?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It does not really help us to look at only one part of the Canadian armed forces and ask about our whole budget. The hon. member has not mentioned the air or the sea personnel, and yet part of the budget goes to them.

I am quite aware of the other branches of the armed forces, and I am not trying to say that the budget does not cover them, but I am saying that our armed forces are consolidated. Is the minister satisfied that that is all we can do with that budget?
We have 22 million people, we have an annual budget of $24 million, and we have a total of 79,000 men in the armed forces. Is that good enough, and is the minister satisfied with that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think we would never be satisfied if we only considered the sharp end unrelated to the support side. We want to increase the sharp end, and I believe this is what the hon. member is talking about. I know something of his background to which he referred, and also his active participation in the militia, and I think he has a good point. We should put as much emphasis as we can on the sharp end. However, we cannot get along without the support forces, and in coming to the conclusion that he may be trying to reach, he should give consideration to the equipment that is in use. This is something that I have tried to emphasize. Very clearly it is not just the numbers that should be considered, whether they are infantry or sea or air forces. It is not just the numbers that determine the military capability, but numbers with equipment. You
Estimates
have to measure numbers and equipment in order to assess military capability, which is the central objective.

I could not agree more with the minister that one cannot measure military capability only in terms of numbers. My colleague says that our front line troops number about 10,000. I assume that when the minister refers to those troops he means troops with equipment and with back up. My question is: how much lower can the armed forces decrease before the land component of the Canadian armed forces reaches militarily a negligible number of men? Can we sink any lower?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is the issue we are facing. We have our commitments in Canada for internal security; we have our commitments to NATO of 5,000 men; we have our commitment for peacekeeping, and we have to achieve a rotation of those personnel. There have to be training programs. The hon. member is correct. We have reached the level where it is difficult for us to carry out all the tasks we are required to undertake. The forces are double tasked and in some cases, triple tasked in order to carry out the duties expected of them.

I thank the minister for his answer, and I think we have got to the heart of the matter. I hope he will remind his colleagues tomorrow that he has support on this side of the House for the difficulty he is in, and he has a lot of support from the public. I might just end my remarks by reminding the House of a verse quoted back at the time of the Napoleonic wars, Mr. Chairman. It goes like this:
God and the soldier we alike adore
In times of danger-not before
The danger gone-and all things righted
God is forgotten, the soldier slighted.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to participate in this debate a little late, and so I am sure a good deal of what I wanted to say has already been said, but I should like to ask the minister to clarify something.
On page 15-18 of the estimates in the section headed "Contribution to NATO Collective Defence Measures", a rough addition of the figures produces something under $1 billion for capital expenditure. This would presumably be hardware of various kinds, ships, etc. May I ask the minister if this is a budgetary item or a phased purchase program which has been hidden in the $2.36 billion total defence budget, or should I consider that item, something over $800 million, to be part of the total $2.36 billion defence budget for this year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member is looking at the first column on page 15-18 headed "Currently Estimated Total Cost", rather than the actual estimates, but I would have to get clarification from him before I fully understand his point.

Mr. Chairman, it is a case of straightening it out in my own mind. Page 15-18 of the estimates deals with capital expenditures, and under the heading "Contribution to NATO Collective Defence Measures" in the column "Currently Estimated Total Cost" the total comes

October 24, 1974
Estimates
to over $800 million. I should like to ask the minister whether that is a budgetary estimate for a year, or are we talking about a phased projects program in terms of capital expenditure in the NATO program?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I understand the hon. member's question correctly, I would say it is a phased program. The first column gives the total that we intend to spend over a number of years; the second column indicates what has been spent up to March 31, 1974, on that program; the third column shows how much we expect to spend on that program this year, and the fourth column shows what we have still to spend in future years.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, that clarifies the matter. I have heard a considerable amount of debate about whether we should leave this budget as is, Mr. Chairman. It has been an interesting debate because my friends in the Conservative Party have reacted fairly predictably. When we talk about public expenditures there is a tremendous hue and cry, but when we get to the subject of defence they say we are not spending enough money.
If we want to save the taxpayers' money this is the place to do it. I congratulate the government on having gone part way by reducing some of these expenditures. If it would really like to save money, however, it could start with the contribution this country makes to the NATO defence alliance and the 5,200 troops committed to that alliance. If we were to bring the troops home and withdraw that $800 million capital expenditure it would save my constituents a pretty significant amount of money which could go a long way toward increasing pensions and improving social services.
The usefulness of NATO to this country is over, Mr. Chairman, and it is time that this House entered into a serious debate on that subject, instead of a debate about the Sherman tank we are about to purchase.
Ramsey MacDonald talked like that and they all nearly lost their lives.

In reply to the hon. member for Annapolis Valley who suggested that World Federalists were just dreamers, Mr. Chairman, I must say that if we do not start dreaming about world federalism and world order, this kind of debate we are having is pretty futile. We will not have a world.
I should like to commend the government on the contribution the Canadian armed forces have made to the cause of world peace. I think it is time we honoured those men who died in the cause of peace both in the Middle East and on Cyprus, while performing a very difficult role. I hope on Remembrance Day some special tribute will be paid to the soldiers who have the difficult job of being unprotected from both sides in a war. We should pay them the honour that is their due, especially those men who died in the service of world peace.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich raised the matter of the Law of the Sea Conference and I should like to ask the minister a question on that subject. It is very likely that this conference will result in at least a 200 mile limit, plus the continental shelf. That could be a difficult

problem for this country, Mr. Chairman, because we will have to patrol that area. May I ask the minister what plans there are for patrolling the 200 mile limit off the coast of British Columbia? Our naval equipment is probably inadequate, and possibly the wrong type to service a very large area.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for New Westminster for referring to the greatest cost of our peacekeeping. I have said this before. Our greatest loss is the loss of life and the number of men who have been wounded in peacekeeping service. I felt that strongly when I attended the funeral of Private Berger in Rimouski. I will be in Lahr, Germany, on Armistice Day, and I will recall there the sentiments which have been expressed here tonight.
Concerning the Law of the Sea Conference, we know that a final decision has not been made. The next conference is ahead of us, and we are preparing to do what we can to implement any new understandings and protect Canadian Interests within the limits finally determined at that conference.

My last point concerns the approximate $54 million being spent on defence research. We should examine the effects of grants given for defence research. When you develop a defence industry which depends on these grants, and admittedly in Canada the risk is small at present, you can run into the sort of thing which happened with the Arrow in Toronto. That aircraft was developed directly because a military-industrial complex was in existence. We know the agony of the decision to scrap the aircraft.
Let me ask the minister if some of that $54 million which is used for defence research has been responsible for a device known as the sound disorientation device. It is used in the interrogation of prisoners, and is now being used in northern Ireland. Is my information accurate? Are our defence research people making this kind of device, which can be classified as a device of military intelligence rather than military hardware.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have no knowledge of that device. I can confirm the hon. member's figures. We spend about $4.5 million on grants to industry and $3 million to universities. That is part of the total of $54 million which we spend on defence research. The remainder is used to operate our own defence research establishments.

Mr. Chairman, we spend $54 million on defence research but not a penny on peace research. Some organizations in this country do effective and useful work in determining the real causes of war, instead of rattling sabres as some of our friends do. I suggest that we should consider seriously giving grants to organizations which do research into the historical causes of war. If you want to spend money effectively, that would be a good start. Most countries of northern Europe spend money on peace research. It would be a useful change if we spent money on peace instead of on war.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Defence commented about an article in this evening's
October 24, 1974

Ottawa Journal by Robert P. Rothschild. May I continue quoting from that same article:
The sad fact is that they are almost reduced to skin and bones. Muscle in the form of modern equipment is lacking. Increased costs and inflation have meant that there is an ever-decreasing portion of the defence budget that can be devoted to new equipment.
Reducing the strength of the forces without cutting out complete commitments will only mean that they will not be able to carry out their tasks properly. This will inevitably breed frustration with a consequent lowering of morale in all ranks, no matter how well paid the serviceman will be-
-government spending is on the increase. The percentage allotted to national defence is on the decrease. One can hardly escape the feeling that the government does not believe in its own announced defence policy.
Last week I asked if the money for overhauling the Boeing 707 at Winnipeg would be allotted under CAE. As the fund is not mentioned in the estimates, will the minister seek the fund next year? Will these funds come under the defence budget, or will the minister apply to Treasury Board?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, these funds have been approved by Treasury Board. Of course they were not approved when these estimates were prepared. The figures only appear in the estimates after they have been approved by Treasury Board.
Mr. Chairman, some months ago the minister said that his department would go into partnership with Air Canada for transporting military personnel. Has that procedure begun?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand we have not entered into charter arrangements with Air Canada.

Is the department planning to enter into an agreement with Air Canada? The minister made a public announcement on that. May I bring to the minister's attention a brief presented to the government in February, 1972, by the Air Transport Association of Canada about the commercial-military partnership which would conduct air transport operations? Even if the minister faces some difficulties, would he consider reviewing that document again and consulting those people about transporting troops and cargo? Also, can the minister explain what his department's relationship will be with Air Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we have discussed contingency plans with Air Canada but we have not entered into any contract for the carriage of our personnel or supplies. From time to time we make use of commercial airlines, but we have no contractual arrangement on a regular basis.

One further question. Does the Department of National Defence have a program to translate all existing technical documents, training and instructional documents, and schematic drawings into the French language? If there is such a program, may we have a description of what is involved?
Estimates

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is a very long-term program. We are implementing the B and B policy in the department but the program to which the hon. member referred is not actively under way at the present time. It is long term.
Does the minister have any idea what the overall cost will be for Canada? Will these documents be translated in each province, in each depot, and also in our overseas bases?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am certain that the figure for the whole of Canada has not been determined. It has not been determined by us.

Is there any sum included in the estimates this year to provide for translation services? How far back will the department be going in its translation procedure? Will the department be ordering bilingual documents in connection with any new equipment that is required?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is provision in the estimates for the translating of manuals and of information relating to new equipment.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the proceedings today, an opportunity which allows us to make comments and pass judgment on departmental activities, or perhaps, more appropriately, inactivities and expenditures within the Department of National Defence.
The main thrust of concern, care and criticism dealt with has been, and no doubt will continue to be the very obvious attempts by the government to reduce the priority of the National Defence Department in relation to other government departments.
Last weekend I had the pleasure of attending a portion of the annual conference, held in St. Thomas, of District A, Royal Canadian Legion. This conference was attended by over 300 delegates representing the many legion branches in southwestern Ontario.
Countless numbers of members expressed concern, disgust, disappointment and disapproval over recent announcements by the government with respect to present and future programs. This group of highly distinguished citizens expresses a well qualified view that must not go unheard. It is a view for which I have the highest respect and regard, and theirs is a concern that I share.
Let me cite in part a resolution presented and passed at that conference. It reads as follows:
Canada has not the military strength to live up to her present commitments. We of the Legion advocate the maintenance of defence on sea-land-air by virtue of our partnership in the commonwealth, the United Nations and NATO. We strongly object to the cut in Canada's armed forces strength.
This statement accurately reflects the mood of that segment of our society, and no doubt reflects the mood of a great number of Canadians.
Now, Mr. Chairman, having expressed the views of a segment of our society to which we owe a tremendous amount of gratitude, indeed for our whole freedom and democratic way of life, I want to turn to another group of people who are close to the beginning of their lifespan, and
742

October 24, 1974
Estimates
upon whose shoulders our future and Canada's future rests. I refer to the youth of Canada. It has often been said, and rightly so, that the most valuable of all resources in our country is our youth.
I will deal, in particular, with the air cadet league of Canada, without a doubt a most neglected group, whose extreme misfortune it is to be placed at the mercy of a defence department that does so little and appears to be planning to do even less for such a worthwhile sector of our Canadian society.
I am in receipt of a recent letter from Mr. Art Jordon, general manager of the St. Thomas YMCA, and the commanding officer of an air cadet squadron. Some of his remarks are pertinent to this debate. He says:
Your are aware that for the past 11 years our YMCA together with the Air Cadet League of Canada, and the Department of National Defence has sponsored an air cadet squadron in St. Thomas.
It has been and we believe still can be a potent force for good among our young citizens.
Unfortunately, in recent years, about the last three to be exact, we have detected what appears to be diminishing interest in cadets by the Department of National Defence. Promises have been made regarding new training aids, films, uniforms, and the support of girl cadets, yet nothing has happened.
We can readily understand the need to curtail expenses at the government level, but seriously question these curtailments being made at the expense of a program that has proven its value over many years.
Some of our squadron's accomplishments are as follows: 27 private pilots, three glider pilots, 14 senior leaders, three athletic leaders, seven to military college, five to police forces, and 19 to regular armed forces. No less than 1,011 different individuals have served one year or more in the squadron.
This record of service can no doubt be multiplied many times across our country.
It is difficult to believe that we are still attempting to outfit the young people in World War II uniforms and using training aids such as ancient .303 rifles with .22 bores.
Our board of directors want to continue this program but if the senior partner, the Department of National Defence, does not soon take some steps to modernize its part of the operation, then there will not be any way we will be able to continue to interest the young men and women who could well be our leaders of the future.
Some of these criticisms require elaboration. Anyone who has seen an air cadet squadron, a navy or army cadet squadron on recent parade could not help but be aware of the deplorable condition of the cadet uniforms. At this time the cadets are wearing the old blue uniforms, many of them are shabby and most of them ill-fitting.
One can easily imagine the difficulty of trying to recruit young people into an air cadet squadron when candidates see the members trooping around in a finely disciplined manner, yet dressed like refugees from a Sad Sack comic strip.
Poor as they are, the supply of these blue uniforms is running out and there is no existing contract to produce more. So the discouraging problems of dress worsen year by year until, I suppose, cadets are left with no working military uniform at all.
The Department of National Defence must take responsibility for outfitting these cadets in a more reasonable manner. Past promises in this regard have not been kept, so one tends to be suspicious of promises made now or in the future. What is required is action, and the sooner the better, before it is too late.

Let me be more specific. A trial uniform, similar to the one used by the permanent force, came out in 1971. Each cadet squadron was given one new green uniform on a trial basis. However, by the end of the 1972 cadet year it was decided by the Department of National Defence that the cost of this clothing was too great and that a cheaper model had to be found.
After more vacillation, a new uniform concept was presented two years later, in May of 1974, at Montebello. Present was Captain N. McPhee, director of cadets, and representatives of cadet organizations from each province. The tone of the meeting was that although the uniform could have been much better, it should be produced immediately in any case, due to the fact that it was so badly needed. The Defence Department said it could not provide the new uniform for at least another year. Now the thinking appears to be that no new uniform will be available before 1977 or 1978. There have been rumblings in fact that the uniform may not even be acceptable to the Department of National Defence after all, and that still another will have to be found.
It has also come to my attention that rank badges are not available and that they are no longer being made. One commanding officer of a cadet squadron here in the capital city of Ottawa told me that if there were many more officer and NCO changes, rank badges would soon have to be made from odd cloth or scraps of material that might be available. If this is the state of cadets and their uniforms in Ontario, where cadets are considered relatively well off, I do not know what must be happening in some of the less fortunate areas of the western provinces and the maritimes.
Another contentious issue is that concerning girl cadets. I should like to take the opportunity of enumerating some of the problems encountered by these girls, because they are not officially recognized by the Department of National Defence. They have no uniform whatever, unless the squadron not only designs one of its own but is successful in persuading an already overtaxed sponsor to pay for it.
If new uniforms could eventually be produced, will there be one suitable for girls as well? Undoubtedly this will bring about longer delay and will probably result in more expense. The minister must be aware of this. More important, he must be prepared to do something about it.
I have a number of items that I wished to comment on, but in view of the time I shall conclude by saying that I trust the Minister of National Defence and his department will give serious consideration to rethinking their position regarding young cadets in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member for Elgin for his remarks, and particularly for bringing the views of the Legion concerning national defence policy to the floor of the House. With regard to girl cadets I draw his attention to the order paper. If he would look at today's order paper, on page 6, item No. 16 is an act to amend certain statutes to provide equality of status thereunder for male and female persons. Perhaps he has read the bill. It gives official recognition to girl cadets.
October 24, 1974
Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue a line of questioning initiated in part by the hon. member for Vancouver South. How many operational tanks are available to the armed forces in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: From memory, Mr. Chairman, a total of 72 Centurions. I believe there are 32 that are operational in Europe, the balance are in Gagetown. There is a total number in Europe of 51; of that number that are operational, I believe my figure of 32 is correct.

With all respect to the minister, I have been informed that in Wainwright, Alberta, there are about 60 Centurion tanks, housed in hangars, which have been largely cannibalized but which could usefully perhaps, through a program like the Israelis use called Retrofit, be restored to first class fighting machines for considerably less money than it costs to buy a new modern battle tank. Can the minister say how much it would cost to refit one of these Centurion tanks to put it in the kind of condition that the armed forces of Israel have been refitting their tanks to with great success-tanks of American, German and Russian design?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Retrofit that the Israelis have undertaken is, I believe, on the Mark XI Centurions, which is a newer model than the one to which the hon. member referred. Although there may be a possibility of refitting them, I think that is very unlikely. The hon. member should identify the date of the tank and its age, before suggesting that we could do the same thing with older tanks as is done with newer models.

With respect, Mr. Chairman, I put it to the minister that he is the one who should be able to date these tanks that are available to the armed forces of the country. I ask him what vintage are these tanks? Are they the same that the minister of national defence for Australia, Mr. L. H. Barnard, referred to in his very interesting speech in April of this year, which is reported in the Australian Foreign Affairs Record? Are they the same type as the type that the Australians are finding obsolete, or are they still older models than the ones referred to by the Australian defence minister?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe the hon. member is referring to the Mark V tank, which is much older than the Mark XI, the Centurion tank we are using in Europe.

I put it to the minister that if we have a tank that is older than a newer tank that the Australians have found to be obsolete, then why is it that a country with half of our population but with substantially larger armed forces is increasing its military budget substantially and we are not matching them? They find it necessary to replace tanks and long range patrol aircraft, while we are still muddling along with equipment that is older and more obsolete than theirs. What is the reason for this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have talked with the minister of defence for Australia, Mr. Barnard, and I know we are well ahead of Australia in terms of replacement of long range patrol aircraft.

That we are well ahead of Australia is certainly a revelation. Is it not true that we are still

seriously considering replacing the Argus with 707s, which are nothing but converted passenger airliners but without the low level surveillance capability of the Argus?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall take only two or three minutes. One of the pieces of legislation which the Minister of National Defence administers is the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act. This is the act under which long-service members of the armed forces receive their pensions. It is similar to the Public Service Superannuation Act, although there are some differences. Another act which is almost parallel to the Canadian Armed Forces Superannuation Act is the RCMP Superannuation Act.
I am not going to launch into a discussion of the various things that might be at fault in the armed forces pension legislation, but there is one point that is very annoying to many retired servicemen. It has to do with the annual escalation of pensions which applies to retired public servants, retired members of the RCMP, and retired armed forces personnel. There is a stipulation that, no matter what one's age when he retires, he cannot draw the escalation until he reaches age 60.
There is a slight qualification in that if one is 55 years of age or over and has 30 years of service he can qualify right away. As the lower ranks have pointed out, this favours those in the higher ranks and discriminates against those in the lower ranks, because those in the lower ranks are forced to retire early.
This is a broad subject and I know that one superannuation plan cannot get out of step with another, but I implore the Minister of National Defence to lock arms with his colleague, the Solicitor General, who is responsible for the RCMP, and for the two of them to have a conference with the President of the Treasury Board. He is new, and this is a good time for him to do something worthwhile. This is a good time for him to make the necessary adjustments so that when servicemen and RCMP personnel are retired in the normal course they might draw their annual escalation without having to wait until age 60. May I ask the minister if he will consider this

in concert with the Solicitor General and make the necessary representations to the President of the Treasury Board?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, I will be glad to do that.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

Mr. Chairman, along the lines of the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I should like to ask a question regarding the thousands of members of the Canadian armed forces who have retired and entered the Public Service of Canada immediately upon retirement. Many of them find themselves now in the position of having worked their entire lives in the Public Service, one part in the armed services and the other part on the civilian side, and are unable to count their service for leave purposes in the Public Service of Canada.
Again, in the same vein as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I ask if the minister would undertake that he will bring to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board the inequity which seems to exist in respect of these people who have served Canada in another capacity and are now continuing their service in the Public Service? I merely ask for that undertaking from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence

He is involved with all of us, and I think I can give an assurance that the matter the hon. member has raised is being given serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for recognizing me, though I regret the indication that I only have enough time for one question. Perhaps I might cite one case that has come to my attention recently. It involves the widow of a serviceman who spent almost his entire adult life in the armed forces. He died, and left her to fend for herself against continuing and rising inflation. She was advised that his military pension had been cut in half. Surely the minister recognizes, as do the officials of his department, that one person cannot get by adequately on half a pension. I am wondering whether the minister is causing this to be reviewed, particularly on behalf of widows with dependents. We all look forward to some positive measures to assist persons in such a predicament.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few moments to briefly discuss some of the problems and interests of the three branches which comprise the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. These are the Indian and Eskimo Affairs Program, the Conservation Program, and the Northern Development Program.
First, I would like to deal with some aspects of the Indian and Eskimo Affairs Program. At the forefront of Indian problems is housing. It is painfully obvious that the program of direct subsidy which the department has been pursuing for some time is simply not keeping up with the demand for housing, especially on reserves.
Many of the houses are substandard, others are rapidly deteriorating. The root of the problem is that virtually all Indian bands and individuals are trying to build houses with only the subsidy money, without making any contribution of their own. This contribution would provide the wherewithal to build better houses and the incentive to keep them in good repair. Good housing lies at the heart of progressive community development because of its total effect on peoples' lives.
Because of the high priority I attach to housing, I was glad to find that housing policy was urgently under review in the department. The National Indian Brotherhood had input into the review through its housing brief, which it presented last April. I was personally disappointed in this proposal by the National Indian Brotherhood because its virtually exclusive thrust was to seek a substantial increase in direct subsidies from the federal government. It seems to me that the subsidy system has demonstrated its weaknesses.
Not only do the funds fall short of its actual need but, even more important, there is absolutely no incentive for the Indian occupant to maintain or improve the home when he does not have one cent of his funds invested in it. My response to the National Indian Brotherhood has, therefore, been to emphasize the co-operative aspects needed for a sound Indian program. They have requested a meeting with me later in November to review thoroughly this whole area. I look forward to meeting with the executive of the National Indian Brotherhood at that time.
However, I do believe that full use should be made of all government programs which are available to assist in the housing area. This has not been done in the past. These programs-whether we are talking about senior citizens housing, low income rental housing, or home improvement programs-all provide alternative sources of assistance for the Indian people. These should be combined with assets the bands have to contribute, and with the individual Indian's ability to pay as well. I look forward to developing jointly proposals for a program along those lines, a program that will be largely under the control of the Indians themselves at the band level.
In the area of economic development my approach has been to follow the same line of reasoning. I am all in favour of deploying government funds so that much needed economic activity can be generated in the Indian communities, in line with the aims and needs of the people concerned and largely under their control. But the govern-
Estimates
ment's contribution to this activity should be combined with contributions the Indian people can make themselves. The government's contribution should be used as a catalyst, or to provide missing components in schemes of development devised by the bands.
I might also mention here that more needs to be done, and is being done, to ensure that the full range of government program-from all departments and agencies, and at the provincial level-are made available to the Indian people, and that the total federal effort relates to services and programs provided by the provinces. There is a growing awareness on the part of Indian leaders at all levels that they are not taking full advantage of the government approved opportunities that are open to them as Canadians for social and economic advancement. I intend to encourage them by all means to seek to use these benefits for their people.
Viewed in the perspective of the whole country, the Indian people as a group exercise control over substantial assets. This applies to their land base particularly, which is increasingly in demand in this country. Some bands have put their land to productive use and thereby increased their assets. But their example has not been followed by all bands, even those who are occupying lands of significant economic value.
Hon. members, particularly Albertans, my have noticed the development of the Enoch Band. This is a proposed development involving half a million dollars on five square miles of band land. It is my view that Indian bands and Indian individuals should be fully prepared to help themselves by making optimum use of any assets they control. The government and the department can, and will play their part in providing seed funds, technical advice and managerial training. But the objectives of neither the Indian people nor the government will be achieved unless the emphasis on self-help is sustained.
I am seriously concerned about our making rapid progress toward self-reliance whether in the field of Indian housing, economic development, local government or education. It will not be achieved in any of these fields unless or until there is a diminished dependency on direct government subsidy.
In the area of claims, in the past year and particularly during the past few months we have been hearing a lot about land claims. We can expect to hear a lot more about them in the years to come. Most of these claims are the subject of longstanding grievance on the part of native groups, but the fact that they are emerging now in concrete form is the direct fruit of the government's policy of funding research on rights and treaties. That program began in earnest in 1970 and has resulted in comprehensive proposals for land settlement in those areas where native title was not previously extinguished and in a growing number of specific claims relating to certain treaties and the administration of the Indian Act.
To deal with this rapidly expanding activity the department has established an office of claims negotiation, as a branch separated from the Indian and Eskimo Affairs Program and the Northern Affairs Program. The executive director of this office, the Indian Claims Commissioner, and other government representatives concerned with

October 24, 1974
Estimates
claims questions, during recent months have had intensive discussions with various native groups.
In the Yukon negotiations are continuing with the Council for Yukon Indians representing both status and non-status Indians there; in British Columbia there have been separate consultations with both the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs and with the Nishga Tribal Council about their land claims; in the Northwest Territories there have been separate ongoing discussions with the N.W.T. Indian Brotherhood and Innuit Tapirisat about how to approach land settlements there; in northern Quebec representatives of the department have sat in on negotiations between the Quebec authorities and representatives of the Indian and Innuit groups of the James Bay area.
The specific claims have given rise to discussions as well, and some of the issues are very difficult indeed because of the various interests involved. The department is currently reviewing the whole situation with a view to making certain changes in the claims process. I have already expressed my willingness and desire to discuss that process with authorized representatives of the native people.
In the area of relations with native associations, the government continues to attach the greatest importance to its relations with the native associations at national and regional levels. It was for this reason that on October 9 a group of ministers met with members of the executive council of the National Indian Brotherhood to discuss a number of questions of current interest. There will be additional meetings of this kind with the brotherhood- the next one is scheduled for early February. In the interim we are jointly considering the need for supportive services, perhaps in the form of a secretariat, to strengthen this consultative mechanism.
I am confident that improved communication will result from these efforts. Our initial meeting can be regarded as a prototype and forerunner of future consultations at ministerial level with the executive of the National Indian Brotherhood.
The government will be engaged in full consultation on all levels with the native people as we begin to work out the revisions to the Indian Act needed to bring it into line with the current needs and wishes of the people concerned. As you know, the government has funded the National Indian Brotherhood to prepare their recommendations on revisions to the Indian Act. We are looking forward to receiving recommendations in the near future. The government sees these consultations on the Indian Act as the major preoccupation and main focus of its efforts to develop mutually satisfactory relations with the native people, for their benefit and the benefit of Canadians generally.
During the first two months in my portfolio I have been greatly occupied with Indian affairs, but I have tried not to ignore the other areas of major responsibility. During the week of September 28 I made a wide ranging tour of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories where I welcomed the opportunity to meet members of the Territorial government and councils, representatives of native

groups, hamlet councils, the press, and the public at large. In part this was a familiarization tour, but I also wished to learn at first hand about the major preoccupations of northerners at present.
In both territories there was a keen interest and some uneasiness about the major land claims that have been advanced. The native peoples have their own anxieties about the pace and direction of resource development, but other northern residents are just as concerned about possible adverse consequences of putting too much emphasis on native interests in land.
These concerns are linked to other impending events in the territories-the constitutional changes that were brought about during the last session of parliament, the forthcoming elections for the territorial councils, and the public inquiry which Judge Berger is carrying out for the federal government into the Canadian Arctic Gas Pipeline Limited application for pipeline right of way. All these developments are somewhat unsettling perhaps, but in the next year or so they should have the combined effect of setting both territories on a firm course toward a balanced development, based more than ever on the needs and aspirations of northerners themselves.
With regard to the matter of parks I should assure hon. members that the solid progress achieved in recent years in the development of national and historic parks and sites is continuing. New program initiatives for Parks Canada, introduced as "Byways and Special Places", have now been organized as the ARC program, Agreements for Recreation and Conservation. These initiatives complement the traditional national parks and national historic sites programs by introducing a system of linear parks based upon land or water routes important to Canada's history and displaying the best of our scenic resources.
The historic canals, for which my department assumed responsibility during the last two years, are the most obvious initial components of the ARC program in which the federal government has an existing responsibility. Initial reaction has been almost exclusively positive, and two programs will become realities shortly. I expect to bring an agreement to cabinet shortly which will provide for the development of the Rideau and Trent-Severn waterways jointly and co-operatively with Ontario. Other provinces are evaluating the program's concepts according to provincial priorities, and the interest is most encouraging.
Finally, I would mention that it is my intention, so far as resources permit, to accelerate the development of our national historic parks system over the next few years. Like my predecessor I regard the parks policy as one of the major elements in the expanding relationship between the federal and provincial governments, and as one that can contribute heavily to the furtherance of Canada's national wellbeing. In my view there is perhaps no better way to safeguard Canada's future than by doing all we can to conserve our natural and historic heritage from the past.
There is one final comment that I should like to make. I should like to put to rest some of the misconceptions and misunderstandings that various people seem to have about the departmental budget. Before assuming responsibility for Indian Affairs and Northern Development I had heard,
October 24, 1974

as I am sure many hon. members had, that Indian Affairs spent 60 per cent to 70 per cent of its budget on administration costs. I investigated these allegations and I can assure you that there is absolutely no foundation to them.
I find that Indian and Eskimo affairs administrative costs represent approximately 7 per cent of the budget, and this figure compares favourably with that of the government as a whole.
Moreover, while Indian and Eskimo affairs expenditures have risen more than threefold in the past six years, the program's staff has remained almost at the same level it was six years ago. This means that our budget increases have not gone to hiring more civil servants but directly to expanding programs which benefit the Indian people. For 1974-75, 31 per cent of the budget was for education expenditures, 14 per cent for social services, 24 per cent for economic and community development-this includes $60 million which was managed directly by the bands themselves-and 23 per cent for capital expenditures on housing, schools, roads, etc. The final per cent is made up of treaty payments and payments to the superannuation account. The 93 per cent of the budget which is not spent on administration is spent on programs which directly benefit the Indian people.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is a complex and interesting one and there are many other aspects upon which I could make additional comments this evening, but I believe these remarks will give some indication of the areas of interest and concern, and I will be interested at this point in hearing the comments and questions of my colleagues.

Madam Chairman, I rise to say a few words in place of my colleague, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, who had to fulfill some speaking engagements in his constituency for which he had made arrangements a month or so ago, and which he could not change when we found out yesterday that this debate would take place today.
I was trying to calculate how many ministers in charge of Indian Affairs and Northern Development I have heard making Ministerial Maiden speeches since I came to this House 12 years ago, and it seemed to me that, with the exception of the six years that the former minister held this portfolio, we have had just about one minister each year. The same speech has been made, with very few changes, by every minister we have had. We have been told of the improvement each year, how much money was being spent, and that around some mythical corner most of the problems will disappear.
By coincidence, Madam Chairman, just today the House Leader of my party received a telegram from Grand Council Treaty No. 3 Indians at Kenora. I should like to read it into the record, not that what they say is necessarily correct but it is representative of what native people across Canada believe, and of what is true in general if not in this particular case. The telegram reads:
-demand a no vote in tonight's vote to cut our capital projects. We wish to remind you that poor housing has been a factor creating unrest in our area for a number of years as recently as the occupation at Kenora this summer. Unless our requests are realized this discontent-
Estimates
ment will grow and grow until not a day will go by without violence and terror in northwestern Ontario. We will not be the victims of inflation fighting for the government. Our conditions must be improved not ignored. We look to you to support our people by defeating the government's motion tonight.
I believe they are wrong in thinking that the capital moneys to be provided for housing will be cut tonight or any other time, but they are not wrong in their feelings that Indian housing programs in this country have been and are a disaster.
A publication put out within the last month or so by Statistics Canada called "Perspective Canada" was the subject of an article in the Winnipeg Free Press on October 2, 1974, which read in part:
Housing, one of the biggest concerns in recent Indian representations, seems to have actually shown a decline based on a three-fold rating of reserve homes as poor, fair or good.
In 1971, Statistics Canada found that 25.4 per cent of families on reserves needed new houses. In 1965, 19.7 per cent were said to need new homes.
Statistics also show that in 1971, 15.9 per cent of occupied houses needed major repairs. In 1960, 6.8 per cent were found to be in that state.
The agency found that in 1971 51.7 per cent of frame houses and those other than log were good while 20.8 per cent were rated poor. Eight years earlier, 59.4 per cent were rated good and 12.9 per cent were considered poor.
The statistics showing the percentage of Indian houses without electric power and running water are even more sad to relate, Madam Chairman. Tonight the minister lectured us on how he was ready to co-operate and consult with the native people and their associations. If he would refer to the representations made to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development by the National Indian Brotherhood a short time ago, he would find that they complain that they have little if any say in the kind of housing programs developed for the reserves.
In a statement made to the cabinet last April they pointed out that up until now government programs have failed because of inadequate funding, a piecemeal approach, and the historical and still present paternalistic approach. They pointed out that there was a backlog of at least 10,000 housing units in the Indian community, and that in the next five years this will increase to about 15,000 units. They asked that the department or Central Mortgage and Housing develop a program and allocate funds which they would use themselves, deciding where, how and when to build the houses required. They suggested a program spread over the next five years at a cost of something like 400 million.
What they are saying, Madam Chairman, is that they have had enough of the department telling them what to do, when to do it, and how to do it. They want to make the decisions themselves. I should like to hear the minister tell us what his department intends to do for the Indians of this country along these lines.
Having spent the bulk of my time speaking of the need for improved housing on the reserves, I want to spend a minute or two speaking about conditions in the city I represent. I am sure the minister knows that, according to Statistics Canada, the Indian population of my city has grown from 210 people in 1951 to over 5,000 in 1971.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I should like the hon. member to know that I share his concern. I do not like the paternalistic approach, and in my opening remarks I tried to emphasize that the approach has to be a co-operative one.
There is no way that the direct grant subsidy housing is going to meet the housing needs of the Indian people. Madam Chairman, but there are many programs available that are not being capitalized on by the Indian people. The figure mentioned of $400 million over the next five years is not going to be realized through a direct grant program. On the other hand I do not find it a frightening figure if you tie it in with other programs. The hon. member mentioned substandard housing, that lacked plumbing and so on.
I have tried to visit all the reserves. I will try to visit those in the four western provinces, B.C. and northern Ontario on the next long week-end. I have already arranged a meeting with the band council of the Treaty 3 people to whom the hon. member referred.
The point is we must use other programs. Under one upgrading program we pay up to $5,000 for family homes if the family income is less than $6,000. Half that is forgiven as a grant, the other $2,500 must be repaid over about 20 years, I think. I discussed this program at one reserve I visited a couple of weeks ago. I was told that 60 out of 65 houses on the reserve did not have indoor plumbing. When I said that this program would be useful, and that repayments would be only $15 or $20 for the next 15 or 20 years, I was told, "This is not the customary way to do it". Somehow or other we must change these ideas, because there is no way we can help these people with straight grant in aid programs. If we want to help them, we must do it through consultation. Our approach must be cooperative and not paternalistic.

Madam Chairman, I have heard some of the things the minister said ever since coming here. I put a question on the order paper which was answered last week. If my memory serves me right, I asked how many people engaged by the Department of Indian Affairs are employed as teachers in secondary schools, in elementary schools and as teachers' aides. As I remember, the answer was 1576 people are so employed. Yesterday I entered a question on the order paper which has not yet been answered. It asks what percentage of those people are of Indian origin. I have not been given the answer, but if

there are more than 50 I will buy the minister the best dinner one can buy in Ottawa.
Last week the hon. member for the Northwest Territories put on the order paper a detailed series of questions about the number of people employed by the department in the Northwest Territories at various levels, from senior specialist down to casual labourer. He also asked how many people are of native origin. The answer was a shocker, a disgrace. Excluding the people in the lowest paid category, those who are unskilled and untrained, the percentage is less than 5 per cent. That is an optimistic classification.
In short, less than 5 per cent of workers in any category are of native origin. If these people are not discriminated against, and I do not think they are, what an indictment this is of our educational system and of our attempt to bring these people into our society. If the minister really means what he says, let us see some action and hear less of the sort of preaching I have heard in my 12 years here.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I share the hon. member's concern, and I think we are moving in the desired direction. I recall there were roughly 400 Indian students receiving university education when I was working as parliamentary secretary to my predecessor. Today the figure is in excess of 1,200. I am optimistic that, as many of these young people work their way through university, we shall find the ratio moving up very substantially. I look forward to the day when we can say that 100 per cent of the total represents native teachers.

Of course we are all happy that more Indian people are attending universities. Let me just summarize the statistics and I shall be finished. Among Indians and Inuits only 1.7 per cent are receiving a university education compared with 11.9 per cent nationally. So we have done one-tenth as well as for the rest of the population.

Madam Chairman, may I say at the outset that I appreciated some of the new ventures that seem to accompany the new minister as he takes on this portfolio. Some of the statements he made certainly lead us to hope that there will be a new line of action within the department, one that is long overdue. We welcome his plans for integration of programs and incentives, and approve of them. I might say that at this point in time an effort is being made to place an emphasis on incentive and self-help, which is very commendable. But it has an underlying note to it which, as far as I am concerned, is questionable, that is, that it would be very easy to take a hard line and say that the native people have to help themselves to resolve their own difficulties, that if they just do that everything will be well.
That is not going to happen, and I should like to warn the minister that such an approach, carried to the extreme, could be detrimental to the cause of the native people, and that a heavy emphasis on incentives should not imply that unless they meet such and such a requirement they will not get any help from the government.
For example, the minister mentioned the Enoch band and the value of the land base that the Indians hold across the country. The fact is that the economic opportunities to develop the land base are not the same for all Indians across this country, just as they are not the same for all other Canadians. One cannot expect a band in northwestern Ontario, or in some northern community in the prairie provinces or Northwest Territories, to have the same economic opportunities as the Enoch band have possessed. They should not be placed in the same category, or even considered in this way.
While the minister assured us that the administration of his department accounts for only 7 per cent of the over-all estimates of his department, he will have to do a much
Estimates
better P.R. job in getting this story across not only to the native community but to Canadians as a whole. In view of the tremendous bureaucratic structure that the minister ranges over, 7 per cent of the over-all expenditure on administration seems to us to be somewhat out of context.
I want to raise a few questions in regard to housing. The housing situation has been mentioned on many occasions by native people who lack even the most basic amenities and shelter, by Indian leaders who have submitted countless briefs and proposals with little sign of response, by concerned Canadians everywhere who feel that the native housing situation constitutes a blatant act of discrimination in this country, and finally by officials of the department. The following quotation is not from the brief of the National Indian Brotherhood but are the words of the assistant deputy minister at a committee hearing on October 15. He said:
We do know that the need exists in forthcoming years for somewhere in the vicinity of 20,000 homes for Indian people-20,000 houses in roughly the next five years.
He went on to comment on the amount allocated per house, and he said:
Firstly, the quality of the shelter is not adequate because it is virtually an impossibility to build an adequate house for $10,000; and secondly, to cope with the quantum of the need it would be necessary for the government to appropriate a sum of money far in excess of the $27 million per annum which is voted today.
He went on to explain two other points. He said that "in the current fiscal year approximately 2,000 new units will be built and a further 900 renovated. A simple extrapolation would indicate that at this rate it is not a catching-up, it is a falling-behind situation". He also estimated the figure needed at $400 million to bring the housing situation up to par. So we are talking about an estimated need of 20,000 units, whereas this year we are building 2,000. We are talking about a total expenditure need of $400 million, whereas this year we are allocating $27 million, or approximately one-twentieth of the total need.
I know the minister said he is engaged in long-range building proposals and discussion with native leaders, but the situation is such that I do not believe we can rely on long-term planning solely on that basis. There is an emergency, a crisis situation, which exists now. This crisis situation is going to build bitterness, frustration and anger on the part of the native people; this will not be a longterm buildup, we will see it breaking out in the next few weeks, months or a year.
What emergency steps is the minister planning for this winter to cope with this crisis situation? What is he going to do now, in addition to these long-term programs, in the immediate weeks and months ahead to meet the demand of the people who will not have adequate housing this coming winter?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
In relation to the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, I hope I did not leave the impression that I was suggesting a sort of abandonment, because that certainly was not my thought. The emphasis I hope I made was on the idea of co-operation, jointly solving the problems of the Indian people.
On the question of priorities, I made myself rather unpopular with a group of Indians from northern Ontario

October 24, 1974
Estimates
who were down recently asking for additional funds for their lunch program. This is a band which, according to my information, finds itself in the top 10 per cent economically of bands throughout the country. I suggested that I did not see how I could justify giving them additional funds in that area when there were so many other bands in the country who found themselves in very destitute conditions-bands in areas such as northern Saskatchewan and other parts of northern Ontario.
I feel strongly that we in this department should be moving in the direction of establishing priorities. There are some bands relatively well to do, and I do not think we should be providing them with anything like the same funding we are giving the more poor bands. This is the sort of rearranging of priorities I would like to see.
In regard to housing I think the 20,000 figure the hon. lady mentioned compares very closely with the figure suggested by the National Indian Brotherhood. As I said in my earlier remarks, I do not find that figure shocking if you look at it in combination with other programs. The hon. member mentioned 2,000 this year, and 700 or 800-I have forgotten the figure-for upgrading. The program of the native brotherhood proposed 4,000 over the next five years, or a total of 20,000. The 2,000 figure represents roughly half, so we are looking at a little better than double the funding.
If one looks outside the straight grants for housing at other programs, for instance we have been discussing senior citizens' homes, I think he will not find the construction of 4,000 units per annum over the next five years as being unreasonable or out of reach at all. This is something that I should like to move toward. This is the approach we should be taking.
Similarly in upgrading, I think we should be following the program of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I am convinced that the meld of these programs, plus the grants given in our department, will go a long way in the next five years in an attempt to bring the Indian housing program into reasonable condition.

I asked what is to be done to provide for this winter to cover special necessities. That has not been answered. Can the minister tell me how this figure of $27 million for housing has been determined? Why is the amount limited to $27 million? Also can he tell me how the need has been established? On what basis are we to accept a figure of 20,000, 10,000 or 2,000 houses that are to be built this year and in the year ahead? To what areas are these to be allocated? Who makes that decision? How can we be sure that some of the areas most in need of housing will not be overlooked? How are these decisions reached?
In the remarks of the minister I have not heard anything about an adult training program which, it seems to me, would be of great help to the native people themselves. I wonder whether the minister has had discussions with his colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, with regard to the whole question of an on-site adult training program on every reservation where needed, so that the native people may be trained not only as carpenters-not everybody should be trained as carpenters if

there is no work for them-but also as electricians, plumbers, and bookkeepers to keep the accounts in respect of everything that goes on in the band.
These people should be trained in all these fields, not only so that they may be able to carry on construction work on the reserves in order to make themselves more self-sufficient, but also to provide a pool of employment which could be used in other areas.
We have already heard that there is a shortage of 40,000 employees in Alberta. What has the department been doing in this past year to help the native people equip themselves for those 40,000 jobs? What is the department planning in the coming winter months to train the native people, so that they will be ready and available for jobs in the Athabasca oil sands when development starts next spring? The minister can talk about CMHC and the senior citizens' program, but what about integration with departments which train people to be self-employed and make a contribution both on the reserves and outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I was asked where these funds come from. The $27 million figure literally evolved as it was increased. Originally I think the amount was $1,500 per unit, then $5,000 per unit, then $8,500 per unit and now $10,000 odd. I should like to move away from the question of so much per unit.

Apart from the concept of so much per subsidy, how do you determine the need each year? For instance when you say that 20,000 units are required, how do you determine in any one year that there will be only 2,000 built? How do you arrive at the 2,000 figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
There have been studies on this, but basically I think the major restraint is financial, how much in additional funds can be squeezed out of my predecessor now the president of the Treasury Board, to be allocated to this program. I am hopeful that we can squeeze out something above the $27 million figure to which the hon. member referred a few moments ago, for the coming year.
As I said, I want to get away from this concept of so much per unit. We should be looking more in terms of funds going to band councils as regional housing authorities that are assuming more and more responsibility of the kind which the hon. member was asking about, for allocating priorities within their area. This is the direction in which I would like us to move so that it is the Indian people themselves who will be taking the responsibility in this regard. This is being done now in some areas. As I mentioned earlier, this is a subject on which I want to canvass later this month-and I am sure it will take many meetings-the representatives of the National Indian Brotherhood.
Let me get back for a moment to the way in which some of the Indian bands apply this program. The other day I was signing documents for the Fort Alexander band in Alberta, in the riding of the hon. member for Provencher. They had received an allocation of some $30,000. Instead of building three $10,000 homes they divided the whole amount. Six of their members came to me and asked me to sign their guarantee documents with CMHC because they

October 24, 1974

want to borrow $12,000 per unit. A $10,000 house is simply not adequate, and instead of building three inadequate $10,000 houses they will build six $17,000 houses. This is the direction which I would like to see more Indian bands and housing authorities taking.
The hon. member asked about manpower and what we are doing in the area of the oil sands. There is a program currently under way with the Great Canadian Oil Sands operation in McMurray where they are putting a group of people through a 16 week program. In addition, in combination with Alberta manpower, native students are being enrolled in the Alberta vocational centre in Fort McMurray so as to assist in training these people for jobs in the tar sands operation.
I mentioned earlier, when replying to the previous questioner, that there are roughly 1,200 native students taking
Estimates
university courses, and roughly another 8,800 in other forms of post secondary education, a lot of it vocational training of various kinds in community colleges, and so forth. We are not making the progress we would like to see, but we are certainly making far better progress than we made half a dozen years ago, and I hope that half a dozen years from now we will be infinitely better than we are doing now.
